The (constrained) Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(S)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sup_{u\in(0,1]:u^{2}=S}\big\{-u^{-2}\big\}=-\frac{1}{2S},\;\text{ for }\;u^{\circ}(S):=\sqrt{S},\;S\in(0,1], $$

and for $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the relevant form of contract is given by

$$ \displaystyle\xi^{\circ}=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z}=U_{\rm A}^{-1}(y_{0})-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(\Sigma_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}+\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma_{\rm A}\int_{0}^{T}|Z_{t}|^{2}\mathrm{d}\langle X\rangle_{t}, $$

for $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $Z\in{\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ . For any $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and $\xi^{\circ}$ of the previous form, the agent’s best response is given by the maximiser of the (constrained) Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}$ , namely $\nu^{\circ}_{t}=u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})=\sqrt{\Sigma_{t}}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , which allows to achieve the best value $y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}$ . As before, we can compute the dynamics of $X$ and $Y^{y_{0},Z}$ under the optimal effort to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} \displaystyle=u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})\mathrm{d}W_{t},\text{ and }\;\mathrm{d}Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z}=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(|u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})|^{-2}+\gamma_{\rm A}|Z_{t}|^{2}|u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})|^{2}\big)\mathrm{d}t+Z_{t}u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

Defining $L^{\circ}_{t}:=X_{t}-Y_{t}^{y_{0},Z}-h\langle X\rangle_{t}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , the principal’s problem becomes a standard stochastic control problem with a one-dimensional state variable $L^{\circ}$ , controlled through $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and $Z\in{\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ :

$$ \displaystyle\ \sup_{y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}}\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0}),\;\text{ where }\;\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0})=\sup_{\Sigma\in{\cal S}}\sup_{Z\in{\cal V}^{\circ}(\Sigma)}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu^{\circ}(\Sigma)}}\big[U_{\rm P}(L^{\circ}_{T})\big], \displaystyle\ \mathrm{d}L^{\circ}_{t}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\big(|u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})|^{-2}+\gamma_{\rm A}|Z_{t}|^{2}|u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})|^{2}+2h\big|u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})\big|^{2}\big)\mathrm{d}t+u^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})(1-Z_{t})\mathrm{d}W_{t},\;t\in[0,T], $$

with initial condition $L_{0}=x_{0}-U_{\rm A}^{-1}(y_{0})$ .

Comparing (4.2) and (4.3), we clearly need to have equality between the optimal controls to ensure that both problems lead to the same results. This necessitates $u^{\circ}(S)=u^{\star}(\gamma)$ , for $(\gamma,S)\in\mathbb{R}\times(0,1]$ , and we therefore intuit the following correspondence:

$$ \displaystyle S^{\star}(\gamma):=\begin{cases}|\gamma|^{-1/2}&\text{if }\gamma<-1,\\
1&\text{if }\gamma\geq-1.\end{cases} $$

This is in line with the correspondence given by Lemma 3.11 since, for $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ , we clearly have

$$ \displaystyle\argmax_{S\in(0,1]}\bigg\{{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(S)+\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\}=\argmax_{S\in(0,1]}\big\{-S^{-1}+\gamma S\big\}=\begin{cases}|\gamma|^{-1/2}&\text{if }\gamma<-1,\\
1&\text{if }\gamma\geq-1.\end{cases} $$

On the other hand, for $S\in(0,1]$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ , we compute

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S=\dfrac{1}{2}\sup_{u\in(0,1]}\big\{\gamma u^{2}-u^{-2}\big\}-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S=\begin{cases}-|\gamma|^{1/2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S&\text{if }\gamma<-1,\\[5.0pt]
\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\gamma-1-\gamma S\big)&\text{if }\gamma\geq-1.\end{cases} $$

Since $S\in(0,1]$ , we first show that Assumption B is satisfied. Indeed,

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\right\}=-\frac{1}{2S}={\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(S),\quad S\in(0,1], $$

with the minimum achieved for $\gamma^{\star}(S)=S^{-2}$ . This is inline with Lemma 3.13.

#### Remark 4.1.

To solve (4.2) or (4.3), one can compute the principal’s Hamiltonian and write the corresponding HJB equation. Recall that both problems are equivalent, but here, (4.3) may be more straightforward to solve compared to (4.2), where one would need to distinguish cases depending on the value of $\Gamma$ . Through standard techniques, one obtains the following values and efforts for the agent and the principal, respectively,

$$ \displaystyle V_{\rm A}(\xi) \displaystyle=R_{\rm A},\;\text{ for }\;\nu^{\star}\equiv 1\wedge\big(2h+\gamma_{\rm A}\overline{\gamma}\big)^{-1/4},\;\text{ with }\;\overline{\gamma}:=\dfrac{\gamma_{\rm P}}{\gamma_{\rm P}+\gamma_{\rm A}}; \displaystyle\text{ and }\;V_{\rm P} \displaystyle=-\exp\Big(-\gamma_{\rm P}\Big(x_{0}-U_{\rm A}^{-1}(R_{\rm A})-b(0)\Big)\Big),\;\text{ for }\;Z^{\star}\equiv\overline{\gamma},\;\Sigma^{\star}\equiv 1\wedge\big(2h+\gamma_{\rm A}\overline{\gamma}\big)^{-1/2}. $$

One can verify that solving (4.2) lead to the exact same results, but with the optimal sensitivity parameter

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{\star}\equiv-\big|\Sigma^{\star}\big|^{-2}\equiv-\big(1\vee\big(2h+\gamma_{\rm A}\overline{\gamma}\big)\big). $$

### 4.2 A more intricate example

We now consider a model inspired by the demand-response problem introduced and solved by Aïd, Possamaï, and Touzi (2022) [1]. In this model33 3 We will only briefly describe the model here and refer to [1] for further discussion and motivation., the agent can impact, through an admissible control $\nu:=(\alpha,\beta)\in{\cal U}$ , both the mean and the volatility of his electricity consumption for various specific usages, such as heating, air conditioning, etc. His deviation with respect to his original consumption $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ is denoted $X$ , and satisfies:

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\alpha_{s}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d}\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(\beta_{s})\mathrm{d}W_{s},\quad t\in[0,T], $$

where $W$ is a $d$ -dimensional Brownian Motion. The volatility function $\sigma$ in the previous dynamics is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\sigma(b):=(\sigma_{1}\sqrt{b_{1}},\dots,\sigma_{d}\sqrt{b_{d}}),\;b:=(b_{1},\dots,b_{d})\in[0,1]^{d},\;\text{ for }\;\sigma_{k}>0,\;k\in\{1,\dots,d\}. $$

As usual, it is assumed that the principal observes the output process $X$ in continuous time, and therefore its quadratic variation. However, contrary to the previous example, these observations are not sufficient to deduce the agent’s effective effort, notably because of the dimension of the underlying noise compare to the observed processes.

Given an admissible contract $\xi$ , the agent’s expected utility to be maximised is defined as follows,

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm A}(\xi,\nu):=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}\bigg[U_{\rm A}\bigg(\xi+\int_{0}^{T}\big(\kappa X_{t}-c(\nu_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}t\bigg)\bigg],\;\text{ with }\;U_{\rm A}(x)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_{\rm A}x},\;x\in\mathbb{R},\;\gamma_{\rm A}>0,\;\kappa>0, $$

where the cost of effort is given, for any $u:=(a,b)\in A\times B$ with $A:=\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}$ and $B:=\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}$ , by

$$ \displaystyle c(u):=c_{1}(a)+\dfrac{1}{2}c_{2}(b),\;\text{ with }\;c_{1}(a):=\dfrac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\frac{a_{k}^{2}}{\mu_{k}}\;\text{ and }\;c_{2}(b):=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\dfrac{\sigma_{k}^{2}}{\lambda_{k}b_{k}}, $$

for some parameters $\lambda_{k}>0$ and $\mu_{k}>0$ , $k\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ .44 4 Note that here, for computational convenience and illustration purposes, we slightly simplify the model, in particular the sets $A$ and $B$ . Indeed, in the original model, these sets are bounded, which will complicate the agent’s problem in our approach. The principal, who represents an electricity producer/supplier, wishes to incentivise the consumer to decrease the mean and the volatility of his consumption during the contracting period, in order to maximise his expected utility, defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm P}(\xi,\nu):=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu}}\bigg[U_{\rm P}\bigg(-\xi-\theta\int_{0}^{T}X_{t}\mathrm{d}t-\dfrac{1}{2}h\langle X\rangle_{T}\bigg)\bigg],\;\text{ with }\;U_{\rm P}(x)=-\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_{\rm P}x},\;x\in\mathbb{R},\;\gamma_{\rm P}>0,\;h>0,\;\theta>0. $$

If we follow the approach developed in [9], and used in [1], the optimal form of contract is given by

$$ \displaystyle\xi=Y_{T}^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}=U_{\rm A}^{-1}(y_{0})-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal H}_{\rm A}(X_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\big(\Gamma_{t}+\gamma_{\rm A}|Z_{t}|^{2}\big)\mathrm{d}\langle X\rangle_{t}, $$

for $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ , a pair of $\mathbb{R}$ -valued processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ , and where the agent’s Hamiltonian is defined for $(x,z,\gamma)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ by

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}(x,z,\gamma) \displaystyle=\sup_{(a,b)\in A\times B}\bigg\{-a\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d}z+\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma\sigma(b)\sigma^{\top}(b)+\kappa x-c_{1}(a)-\dfrac{1}{2}c_{2}(b)\bigg\} \displaystyle=\kappa x-\inf_{a\in A}\big\{a\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d}z+c_{1}(a)\big\}-\dfrac{1}{2}\inf_{b\in B}\big\{c_{2}(b)-\gamma\sigma(b)\sigma^{\top}(b)\big\}. $$

As usual, computing the optimiser of the Hamiltonian will determine the agent’s best response functions, i.e.

$$ \displaystyle a^{\star}_{k}(z)=-\mu_{k}z\vee 0,\;\text{ and }\;b^{\star}_{k}(\gamma)=(-\lambda_{k}\gamma)^{-1/2},\;\gamma<0,\quad k=1,\dots,d. $$

We can then reformulate the principal’s problem as follows,

$$ \displaystyle\ \sup_{y_{0}\geq R_{\rm A}}\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0}),\;\text{ where }\;\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}(y_{0})=\sup_{(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{\nu^{\star}(Z,\Gamma)}}\bigg[U_{\rm P}\bigg(-Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}_{T}-\theta\int_{0}^{T}X_{t}\mathrm{d}t-\dfrac{1}{2}h\langle X\rangle_{T}\bigg)\bigg], $$

with dynamics of state variables $X$ and $Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}$ under the optimal efforts given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} \displaystyle=-\widebar{\mu}(Z_{t}\wedge 0)\mathrm{d}t+(-\Gamma_{t})^{-1/4}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\dfrac{\sigma_{k}}{\lambda_{k}^{1/4}}\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{k}, \displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}_{t} \displaystyle=\dfrac{1}{2}\bigg(-2\kappa X_{t}+\widebar{\mu}(Z_{t}\wedge 0)^{2}+\widebar{\sigma}\bigg(\sqrt{-\Gamma_{t}}+\gamma_{\rm A}\dfrac{|Z_{t}|^{2}}{\sqrt{-\Gamma_{t}}}\bigg)\bigg)\mathrm{d}t+\dfrac{Z_{t}}{(-\Gamma_{t})^{1/4}}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\dfrac{\sigma_{k}}{\lambda_{k}^{1/4}}\mathrm{d}W_{t}^{k}, $$

for $t\in[0,T]$ , with initial conditions $X_{0}=x_{0}$ and $Y^{y_{0},Z,\Gamma}_{0}=U_{\rm A}^{-1}(y_{0})$ , and where we denoted

$$ \displaystyle\widebar{\mu}:=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k},\;\text{ and }\;\widebar{\sigma}:=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\dfrac{\sigma_{k}^{2}}{\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}}. $$

Alternatively, if we proceed with our approach, the constraint Hamiltonian is given for $(x,z,S)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{\star}_{+}$ by

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}(x,z,S) \displaystyle=\kappa x-\inf_{a\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}\big\{a\cdot\mathbf{1}_{d}z+c_{1}(a)\big\}-\dfrac{1}{2}\inf_{b\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}\text{ s.t }\sigma(b)\sigma(b)^{\top}=S}\big\{c_{2}(b)\big\}, $$

and leads to the following optimiser

$$ \displaystyle a^{\circ}_{k}(z)=-\mu_{k}(z\wedge 0)\;\text{ and }\;b^{\circ}_{k}(S)=\frac{S}{\widebar{\sigma}\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}}. $$

We can then compute the dynamics of $X$ and $Y^{y_{0},Z}$ under the optimal effort, and rewrite the principal’s problem as a more standard control problem, similar to (4.4). It is nevertheless already obvious that, to have equivalence between the two problems, we need to ensure that the quadratic variation of $X$ in both problems coincides, leading to the following relationship between $S\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\star}$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}_{-}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{d}\sigma_{k}^{2}b_{k}^{\circ}(\gamma)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\sigma_{k}^{2}b_{k}^{\star}(\gamma)\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad S=\dfrac{\widebar{\sigma}}{\sqrt{-\gamma}}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\gamma=-\dfrac{\widebar{\sigma}^{2}}{S^{2}}. $$

One can verify that this coincides with the correspondence given by Lemmas 3.11 and 3.13. Indeed, we have

$$ \displaystyle S^{\star}(\gamma):=\argmax_{S>0}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(x,z,S)+\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\} \displaystyle=\argmax_{S>0}\bigg\{-\frac{\widebar{\sigma}^{2}}{S}+\gamma S\bigg\}=\dfrac{\widebar{\sigma}}{\sqrt{-\gamma}},\quad\gamma<0, \displaystyle\text{ and }\;\gamma^{\star}(S):=\argmin_{\gamma<0}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(x,z,\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\} \displaystyle=\argmin_{\gamma<0}\bigg\{-2\widebar{\sigma}(-\gamma)^{1/2}-\gamma S\bigg\}=-\dfrac{\widebar{\sigma}^{2}}{S^{2}},\quad S>0. $$

In particular, Assumption B is satisfied since

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\gamma<0}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(x,z,\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\}=\kappa x+\dfrac{1}{2}\widebar{\mu}(z\wedge 0)^{2}-\dfrac{\widebar{\sigma}^{2}}{S}={\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(x,z,S),\quad S>0, $$

and the minimum is achieved at $\gamma^{\star}(S)$ .

### 4.3 A ‘counter-example’

In this example, we highlight that Assumption B may not always be satisfied, and that, in this case, there may be a difference between:

- • the value of the ‘first-best’ formulation, namely $V^{\circ}_{\rm P}$ in Problem 3, or equivalently $\widetilde{V}^{\circ}_{\rm P}$ in Problem 4,

- • the value of the original problem when restricting to contracts of the form (2.11), i.e. $\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ in Problem 2.

For this, we consider the controlled state equation (4.1) driven by a one-dimensional Brownian Motion $W$ as in the first example in Section 4.1, but where now the control process $\nu$ can take values in $U:=[-1,1]$ . We note that achievable quadratic variations take values in $[0,1]$ . We assume further that the agent’s cost function is given by $c(u)=1-u^{4}$ for $u\in[-1,1]$ , thus non-negative and bounded as required.

We first highlight that Assumption B is not satisfied in this framework. Indeed, let $S\in[0,1]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(S):=\sup_{u\in U:u^{2}=S}\big\{-c(u)\big\}=\max\Big\{\big(\sqrt{S}\big)^{4}-1,\big(-\sqrt{S}\big)^{4}-1\Big\}=S^{2}-1,\quad\text{ for }\;u^{\circ}(S)=\pm\sqrt{S}. $$

The ‘constraint’ Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}$ is proper, continuous, but convex instead of concave, implying that Assumption B is not satisfied for all $S\in[0,1]$ . Indeed, for any $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma) \displaystyle:=\sup_{u\in U}\bigg\{\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma u^{2}-c(u)\bigg\}=\sup_{S\in[0,1]}\bigg\{\sup_{u\in[-1,1]:u^{2}=S}\bigg\{\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma u^{2}+u^{4}\bigg\}\bigg\}-1=\sup_{S\in[0,1]}\bigg\{\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S+S^{2}\bigg\}-1 \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\gamma/2&\mbox{ if }\gamma>-2,\text{ for }S^{\star}(\gamma)=1,\text{ i.e. }u^{\star}(\gamma)\in\{-1,1\};\\
-1&\mbox{ if }\gamma=-2,\text{ for }S^{\star}(\gamma)\in\{0,1\},\text{ i.e. }u^{\star}(\gamma)\in\{-1,0,1\};\\
-1&\mbox{ if }\gamma<-2,\text{ for }S^{\star}(\gamma)=0,\text{ i.e. }u^{\star}(\gamma)=0.\end{cases} $$

Computing the convex conjugate of ${\cal H}_{\rm A}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\}=S-1,\quad\text{ for }\gamma^{\star}=-2. $$

We thus have

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma S\bigg\}-{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(S)=S-S^{2}, $$

which is always non-negative, but (strictly) positive on $(0,1)$ . In other words, Assumption B is not verified, unless we restrict the study to $S\in\{0,1\}$ . Intuitively, if the principal’s optimal choice for the quadratic variation is at either $S=0$ or $S=1$ , then no issue should arise, since Assumption B is satisfied at these two points. However, if the optimal value for the quadratic variation lies in the interior of the interval $(0,1)$ , the ‘first-best’ value should exceed the value obtained by restricting to contracts of the form (2.11). Indeed, as highlighted above when computing the maximisers of the Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\rm A}$ , these contracts can only incentivise optimal efforts taking values in $\{-1,0,1\}$ , thus leading to a quadratic variation taking values in $\{0,1\}$ only. We confirm this intuition below.

We consider the following criterion for the principal, in which the cost function $c_{\rm P}$ will be chosen later,

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm P}(\xi,\Sigma):=\mathbb{E}\bigg[X_{T}-\xi-\int_{0}^{T}c_{\rm P}\big(\Sigma_{t}\big)\mathrm{d}t\bigg]. $$

In the ‘first-best’ formulation, we know that the optimal contract form is given by

$$ \displaystyle\xi=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{T}{\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})\mathrm{d}t+\int_{0}^{T}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}X_{t}, $$

where the pair of processes $(Z,\Sigma)$ has to be chosen by the principal. The optimal efforts are given by the maximiser of the constrained Hamiltonian ${\cal H}^{\circ}_{\rm A}$ , here $\nu_{t}^{\circ}=\pm\sqrt{\Sigma_{t}}$ , which leads to ${\cal H}_{\rm A}^{\circ}(\Sigma_{t})=\Sigma_{t}^{2}-1$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , as shown in (4.5). Using the dynamics of $X$ and $\xi$ under these optimal efforts, we can compute

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm P}(\xi,\Sigma)=x_{0}-y_{0}-T+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\big(\Sigma_{t}^{2}-c_{\rm P}(\Sigma_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}t\bigg]. $$

By pointwise optimisation, the optimal $\Sigma$ should be given by

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{t}^{\star}\in\argmax_{S\in[0,1]}\big\{S^{2}-c_{\rm P}(S)\big\},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

Now, by choosing the cost function $c_{\rm P}(S)=S^{3}$ , we obtain a maximum at $4/27$ achieved for $S^{\star}=2/3\in(0,1)$ . In other words, the optimal quadratic variation is neither $0$ or $1$ , and one can thus expect a duality gap in this case.

Indeed, one can also compute the principal’s value when she can only offer contracts of the form (2.11). In this case, we still consider the criterion (4.7), but with the difference that $\Sigma$ is not directly chosen by the principal. In particular, given a contract of the form (2.11) indexed through a parameter $\Gamma$ , we have $\Sigma_{t}=|u^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}$ , $t\in[0,T]$ , where $u^{\star}$ is defined through (4.6) as the maximiser of the Hamiltonian ${\cal H}_{\rm A}$ . Using this contract form and the associated optimal efforts, we can then compute

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm P}\big(\xi,|u^{\star}(\Gamma_{\cdot})|^{2}\big)=x_{0}-y_{0}+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{T}\bigg({\cal H}_{\rm A}(\Gamma_{t})-\dfrac{1}{2}\Gamma_{t}|u^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}-c_{\rm P}\big(|u^{\star}(\Gamma_{t})|^{2}\big)\bigg)\mathrm{d}t\bigg], $$

where now the process $\Gamma$ has to be chosen optimally. Again by pointwise optimisation, we should have

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{t}^{\star}\in\argmax_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma|u^{\star}(\gamma)|^{2}-c_{\rm P}\big(|u^{\star}(\gamma)|^{2}\big)\bigg\},\quad t\in[0,T]. $$

By choosing $c_{\rm P}(S)=S^{3}$ as before, the maximisation problem becomes

$$ \displaystyle\max_{\gamma\in\mathbb{R}}\bigg\{{\cal H}_{\rm A}(\gamma)-\dfrac{1}{2}\gamma|u^{\star}(\gamma)|^{2}-|u^{\star}(\gamma)|^{6}\bigg\}=-1,\quad\text{for }\;\gamma^{\star}=-2. $$

Therefore, while the value in the ‘first-best’ case is given by $x_{0}-y_{0}-23T/27$ , the maximum possible value achievable with the contracts (2.11) in the original ‘second-best’ problem is lower, equal to $x_{0}-y_{0}-T$ .

This illustrative example highlights that if Assumption B does not hold, the contract form (2.11) may fail to achieve the ‘first-best’ value. As mentioned in Remark 3.12, without Assumption B, the proof of optimality of the contract form (2.11) via 2BSDEs may also break down. Therefore, while this example illustrates a difference between the value of the original problem when restricting attention to contracts of the form (2.11) (namely, Problem 2) and the value of the ‘first-best’ reformulation (Problems 3 and 4), it remains unclear whether this reflects an intrinsic ‘gap’ between Problem 1 and Problem 3, or whether it is possible to design a new class of penalisation contracts to bridge this gap. We believe this is a very interesting question, which we leave for further research.

## 5 Conclusion

Principal–agent problems with volatility control are notoriously challenging to study. Specifically, the only existing approach so far, introduced by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [9], relies on the sophisticated theory of second-order BSDEs. More precisely, the authors establish the equality between the principal’s value $V_{\rm P}$ in the original problem (Problem 1) and the value $\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ of a more standard stochastic control problem (Problem 2). While it is clear from the restriction to contracts of the form (2.15) that $V_{\rm P}\geq\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}$ , the converse inequality requires to prove that such restriction is without loss of generality, which necessitates the use of second-order BSDEs. Even though this approach indeed allows a thorough analysis of the principal–agent problem with volatility control, and therefore of the applications arising from this framework, the mathematical complexity of this approach hampers the study of natural and relevant extensions, especially to multi-agent frameworks. Moreover, this mathematically challenging approach also prevents a wider dissemination of these models and their relevant applications in many fields, from operation research to economics.

In contrast, the novel approach we develop only relies on the theory of BSDEs, thanks to the introduction of a ‘first-best’ counterpart of the original problem, in which the principal directly controls the density of the output’s quadratic variation (Problem 3). This alternative problem is purely theoretical: it can be seen as a dual to Problem 1, and is not necessarily meaningful in terms of application. Nevertheless, compared to Problem 1, Problem 3 can be solved in a more straightforward way, following the so-called Sannikov’s trick. More precisely, one can prove using BSDEs that the restriction to contracts of the form (3.13) is without loss of generality, which implies that the principal’s problem in this ‘first-best’ reformulation is actually equivalent to another standard stochastic control problem, namely $\widetilde{V}_{\rm P}^{\circ}$ defined in Problem 4. It then remains to show that the value $V_{\rm P}^{\circ}$ of the ‘first-best’ reformulated problem, which naturally satisfies $V_{\rm P}^{\circ}\geq V_{\rm P}$ , can be achieved. For this, it suffices to use the contract form (2.11) considered in [9], and thus show that Problem 2 and Problem 4 are actually equivalent. As a result, instead of choosing the sensitivity parameter $\Gamma$ in the contract form (2.11), one can directly optimise the density process $\Sigma$ of the output’s quadratic variation. Conversely, given a density process $\Sigma$ , one can recover from the correspondence in Lemma 3.13 the appropriate pay-for-performance sensitivity $\Gamma$ in the contract form (2.11). We finally obtain that the problems introduced throughout this paper are all equivalent under our standing Assumptions A and B, which is graphically summarised by Figure 1.

*Figure 1: Equivalence of the problems*

We nevertheless remark that, at the end, and depending on the framework under consideration, Problem 2 may still be easier to solve than Problem 4. Indeed, as illustrated through Section 4, the agent’s problem Problem 4 involves a constrained optimisation, making it potentially more complex to solve in practice. However, this does not undermine the effectiveness of our approach, since its main goal is to provide a theoretically simpler method to establish the optimality of the relevant contract form. Ultimately, since all problems are equivalent, this approach offers the flexibility to choose the most practical problem to solve. We also emphasise that the contract form (2.11), originally introduced in [9], is essential for proving the equivalence between the original problem and its ‘first-best’ reformulation. Nevertheless, the key message of our approach is that we do not need to rely on 2BSDEs to demonstrate the optimality of these contracts; their optimality naturally comes from the fact that they allow the principal to achieve the best utility possible.

We believe that this alternative, simpler approach will provide a more straightforward pathway for extending principal–agent problems to more complex frameworks, involving for example multi-agent settings, mean-field interactions, or non-continuous output processes. For instance, solving principal–multi-agent problems with volatility control via the original approach in [9] requires the consideration of ‘multidimensional 2BSDEs’, as highlighted in [18], for which the theory is actually not yet developed. In contrast, following our proposed approach, one could rely on the more mature theory of multidimensional BSDEs to show the equivalence between the original problem and its ‘first-best’ reformulation, thereby ensuring optimality of appropriate revealing contracts without relying on multidimensional 2BSDEs. Furthermore, this simplified approach shall facilitate practical and more widespread implementation of principal–agent problems with volatility control in diverse fields, beyond mathematical finance.

To conclude, we want to emphasise that while our approach provides a simpler and more accessible framework for solving principal–agent problems with volatility control, it relies on two key assumptions: Assumption A, which guarantees weak uniqueness and thus enables the use of the martingale representation theorem, and Assumption B, under which the contract form proposed in [9] remains optimal. First, we view Assumption A as relatively mild and well motivated, particularly given the intended applications. Indeed, without weak uniqueness, the same choice of effort by the agent could generate different distributions for the controlled output process, making the model less meaningful from an economic standpoint. Moreover, although this assumption is central to our current BSDE-based arguments, it may be possible to relax it by considering generalised BSDEs, i.e. with an orthogonal martingale component. This approach would still remain simpler than the general 2BSDE framework, and could be extended for example to multi-agent settings, thanks to the existence of multi-dimensional versions of such BSDEs. Second, we have strong reason to believe that our main result, Theorem 3.10, will remain valid even without Assumption B. However, since the contract form from [9] may no longer be optimal in this case, this would require constructing a new class of contracts. While preliminary exploration in this direction is promising, a full rigorous treatment is left for future research.

# Forcing and duality-corrected contracts for volatility control

**Authors:** Alessandro Chiusolo ††thanks: Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering (ORFE), Princeton University, USA.††thanks: Research partially supported by the NSF grant DMS-2307736. Emma Hubert 22footnotemark: 2 ††thanks: CEREMADE, Université Paris–Dauphine, PSL Research University, France. Dylan Possamaï ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, ETH Zürich, Switzerland. ## Abstract

In this paper, we revisit the construction of optimal incentives in continuous-time principal–agent problems with drift and volatility control. Originally, a general approach relying on dynamic programming and second-order backward stochastic differential equations (2BSDEs) was developed by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [8] to determine the optimal form of contracts in this setting. More recently, Chiusolo and Hubert (2026) [5] proposed a BSDE-based approach by introducing an alternative ‘contractible-volatility’ problem for the principal. In addition to the proposed new method, this work highlights that the optimality result of [8] actually hinges on an assumption—stated below as Assumption 2.3—which may not hold in general. Motivated by this, we introduce in this paper a more general class of contracts, parametrised by a function $\psi$ subject to conditions that make the contract revealing for the agent and without loss of generality for the principal. We further provide two natural specifications of $\psi$ : one, inspired by the BSDE approach, yielding a forcing-type contract; the other, motivated by the 2BSDE approach, correcting the duality gap when Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied.

## 1 Introduction

Principal–agent problems originate in the economic literature on optimal incentives under asymmetric information, particularly in the context of moral hazard. The foundational literature was shaped by the influential contributions of Mirrlees in [18] (1976) and [19] (1999), Holmström (1979) [13], and Grossman and Hart (1983) [11]. More precisely, in these models a principal (she) is imperfectly informed about the efforts of an agent (he), and seeks to incentivise him to undertake appropriate actions over a given period. To that end, the principal can design a contract, usually represented by a terminal payment $\xi$ at a finite time horizon $T>0$ , and indexed on what she can observe. In particular, in a continuous-time stochastic framework, it is usually assumed that the agent can choose some control process unobservable by the principal, but impacting the drift and/or the volatility of an observable output, represented by a stochastic process $X$ . The goal of the principal is therefore to determine an optimal contract, as a function of the trajectories of $X$ , in order to maximise her expected utility, and anticipating the agent’s optimal response to this contract. It is also commonly assumed that the agent will decline the contract proposed by the principal if his resulting utility falls below a given level, defined as his reservation utility, thus adding a constraint for the principal in her design problem. For classical textbook treatments of principal–agent models, see Laffont and Martimort (2002) [17], Bolton and Dewatripont (2005) [3] and Salanié (2005) [23].

Originally introduced by Holmström and Milgrom (1987) [14], continuous-time versions were later generalised by Sannikov (2008) [24]. His approach—coined Sannikov’s trick in the associated literature—consists in using the agent’s continuation utility to determine the optimal form of terminal payments, and further consider it as an additional state variable for the principal. Since then, continuous-time contract theory has been the subject of an extensive literature, with overviews provided in the monographs by Cvitanić and Zhang (2012) [6] and Sung (2023) [25]. In a drift control framework, this continuation utility can naturally be related to the first component of the solution to a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) by standard stochastic control theory. When adding the possibility for the agent to impact the volatility of the output process, this continuation utility now has to be related to a second-order backward stochastic differential equation (2BSDE), as shown by Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2018) [8]. More precisely, in this paper, the relevant form of contracts is shown to be indexed on the trajectory of the output $X$ through a process $Z$ chosen by the principal—as in the classical drift control case—but also on its quadratic variation $[X]$ , through an additional process $\Gamma$ also chosen by the principal. Informally, while indexing the contract on the output process $X$ incentivises the agent to undertake some efforts on the drift, the indexation on its quadratic variation encourages the control of the volatility. In the end, they prove that the original principal’s optimisation problem boils down to a more standard stochastic control problem, with two state variables $X$ and $\xi$ controlled by the pair $(Z,\Gamma)$ .

Very recently, Chiusolo and Hubert (2026) [5] presented an alternative approach to proving the optimality of the contract form introduced in [8], within the same general framework. This approach, which is based solely on BSDE theory, consists in defining another optimisation problem for the principal, called ‘first-best’, in the sense that there is no moral hazard on the quadratic variation of the output process. More precisely, while in the original problem the agent controls the drift and the volatility of the stochastic process $X$ , the alternative one consists in assuming that, since the quadratic variation is observable in continuous-time, it can be directly controlled by the principal, who can in turn force the agent to achieve a specific choice. Note that the term first-best in principal–agent problems commonly refers to a setting without moral hazard, in which the principal directly chooses the agent’s controls, as opposed to second-best. To avoid confusion, we depart slightly from the terminology in [5] by using here the term contractible-volatility to designate this alternative problem. There, the principal thus chooses both a contract $\xi$ and the density with respect to the Lebesgue measure of the quadratic variation, later denoted $\Sigma$ , to which the agent replies with an effort constrained to achieve the specific density $\Sigma$ fixed by the principal. The advantage is that this alternative problem can be solved by following Sannikov’s trick, thus relying solely on BSDEs. Then, using the contract form proposed in [8] in the original problem, it can be shown that the principal actually achieves her contractible-volatility value, which is the maximum possible value, thus ensuring optimality of the contract form introduced in [8] and equivalence between the original and the alternative problems.

However, as highlighted in [5], the equivalence between the two formulations—hence the two approaches—holds only under Assumption 2.3. More importantly, the main result of [8], namely Theorem 3.6 establishing the optimality of the proposed contract form, may fail when this assumption does not hold. While Assumption 2.3 is sufficient to guarantee optimality of the original contract form and is satisfied in most examples considered in the literature, it remains crucial to investigate the existence of optimal contracts beyond this setting, in order to reach a comprehensive understanding of optimal incentives in continuous-time principal–agent problems with volatility control. From an economic perspective, when this assumption is not satisfied, it remains unclear whether the principal can still attain her value in the corresponding contractible-volatility alternative problem introduced in [5].

We show in this paper that, even when Assumption 2.3 does not hold, one can still identify an optimal form of contracts, in the sense that they are revealing for the agent and that restricting the study to this specific form is without loss of generality for the principal. The intuition behind this contract form arises from the 2BSDE methodology developed in [8], but the BSDE approach from [5] can also be used to establish its optimality. In particular, this proves that the contractible-volatility value—in the sense of the first-best problem in [5]—can always be attained. More precisely, our study yields the following main contributions.

$(i)$ Where the 2BSDE proof can fail. We remind one of the main findings of [5], namely the exact obstruction in the 2BSDE route of [8]: in order to identify a process $\Gamma$ satisfying the identity (3.14), i.e.

$$ \dot{K}_{t}+F_{t}\big(X_{\cdot\wedge t},Y_{t},Z_{t},\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}\big)=H_{t}\big(X_{\cdot\wedge t},Y_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t}\big)-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\big[\Gamma_{t}\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}\big], $$

one needs both the equality $F=F^{\star\star}$ (where the Fenchel transform is taken with respect to the squared volatility variable) and attainment of the infimum by a measurable selector $\gamma^{\star}$ as in Assumption 2.3. Absent these, the density $\dot{K}$ of the 2BSDEs non-decreasing process cannot always be encoded by some $\Gamma$ , and [8, Theorem 3.6] may fail.

$(ii)$ A general $\psi$ –parametrised contract class. We introduce a contract class that specifies the density $\dot{K}$ in the 2BSDE (3.1) as $\dot{K}_{t}=\psi_{t}\big(X_{\cdot\wedge t},Y_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}\big)-F_{t}\big(X_{\cdot\wedge t},Y_{t},Z_{t},\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}\big)$ , where for $E$ an arbitrary space,

$$ \inf_{S}\{\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\}=0,\;\min_{\gamma\in\text{$E$}}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=F_{t}(x,y,z,S),\;\text{and}\;\sup_{\gamma\in\text{$E$}}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=+\infty. $$

The first condition normalises payments at the realised volatility so that the contract is revealing (see Proposition 3.3), while the second and third ones give the principal full reach over non-negative $\dot{K}$ , and yields the without loss of generality reduction (see Theorem 3.7). Under Assumption 2.3, $\psi$ can be chosen to recover the classical contracts of [8].

$(iii)$ Equality with the contractible-volatility problem. Let $V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ be the principal’s value in the auxiliary problem where $\Sigma$ (the density of $[X]$ ) is selected by the principal, and $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ the value in the original problem. Proposition 3.10 gives a correspondence between feasible $(\Sigma,Z)$ and $(Z,\Gamma,\psi)$ , thus ensuring that $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}=V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ , even without Assumption 2.3.

$(iv)$ Two canonical, economically transparent contracts. The contract form we propose has the drawback of being inherently non-unique, since it is written in terms of a function $\psi$ that may be chosen arbitrarily within a very broad class. Nevertheless, we exhibit in Section 4 two concrete and robust contract specifications: forcing contracts, obtained by penalising observable quadratic deviations to ‘target’ $\Sigma$ ; and duality–corrected contracts, which add the explicit gap $F^{\star\star}-F$ to the original contract form in [8].

$(v)$ Examples and counterexamples. We revisit the counterexample from [5], and show that our contracts attain the contractible-volatility value. We also remark that several explicit models in the literature satisfy Assumption 2.3, but provide another counterexample within the framework of Cvitanić, Possamaï, and Touzi (2017) [7].

The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the general model and then briefly recall the two existing approaches, developed in [5, 8]. In Section 3, we introduce a more general form of contracts, proving their optimality even when Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied. More precisely, Section 3.2 states the main results, on the revealing property of such contract form in Proposition 3.3 and the fact that the restriction to this form is without loss of generality from the principal point of view in Theorem 3.7. The latter is then rigorously proved in Section 3.3, relying on both approaches. Section 4 introduces two canonical examples of contracts. Finally, in Section 5, we review some of the existing models from the literature.

Notations. Let $\mathbb{N}^{\star}\coloneqq\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}$ be the set of positive integers. For any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ , we will denote by ${\cal S}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ (respectively ${\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ ) the set of symmetric (resp. symmetric positive semi-definite) $n\times n$ matrices with real entries. For any matrix $S\in{\cal S}_{n}^{+}(\mathbb{R})$ , we will denote by $S^{1/2}$ its $(n,n)$ -dimensional symmetric square root, and by $S^{-1/2}$ its pseudo-inverse. For fixed time horizon $T>0$ , representing the maturity of the contract, we let ${\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n})$ denote the set of continuous functions from $[0,T]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . The set ${\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n})$ will always be endowed with the topology associated to the uniform convergence on the compact $[0,T]$ . For a probability space of the form $\Omega\coloneqq{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n})$ and an associated filtration $\mathbb{F}$ , we will have to consider processes $\psi:[0,T]\times\Omega\longrightarrow E$ , for some Polish space $E$ , which are $\mathbb{F}$ -optional, i.e. ${\cal O}(\mathbb{F})$ -measurable where ${\cal O}(\mathbb{F})$ is the so-called optional $\sigma$ -field generated by $\mathbb{F}$ -adapted right-continuous processes. In particular, such a process $\psi$ is non-anticipative in the sense that $\psi(t,x)=\psi(t,x_{\cdot\wedge t})$ , for all $t\in[0,T]$ and $x\in\Omega$ . Throughout the paper, and as is customary in the probabilistic literature, we will omit to write explicitly the dependence of such processes on the canonical process $X$ , and simply write $\psi_{t}$ instead of $\psi_{t}(X_{\cdot\wedge t})$ , whenever no confusion can arise. Furthermore, for any filtration $\mathbb{F}\coloneqq({\cal F}_{\text{$T$}})_{t\in[0,\text{$T$}]}$ and probability measure $\mathbb{P}$ , we will denote by $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{P}}\coloneqq({\cal F}_{\text{$T$}}^{\mathbb{P}})_{t\in[0,\text{$T$}]}$ the usual $\mathbb{P}$ -completion of $\mathbb{F}$ ; $\mathbb{F}^{\text{$+$}}\coloneqq({\cal F}_{\text{$T$}}^{\text{$+$}})_{t\in[0,\text{$T$}]}$ the right limit of $\mathbb{F}$ ; $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$+$}}}\coloneqq({\cal F}_{\text{$T$}}^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$+$}}})_{t\in[0,\text{$T$}]}$ the augmentation of $\mathbb{F}$ under $\mathbb{P}$ . Finally, for technical reasons, we work under the classical ZFC set-theoretic axiom. This is a standard widely used in classical stochastic analysis theory (see Dellacherie and Meyer (1978) [9, Chapter 0.9]). We also rely on the continuum hypothesis, which is needed to apply the aggregation result of Nutz (2012) [20].

## 2 Model and previous results

We first recall the framework introduced in [8, 5], and then outline their respective 2BSDE- and BSDE-based approaches.

### 2.1 General framework

Throughout the paper, fix some positive integer $d\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$ and $T>0$ a finite time horizon, and let $X$ be the canonical process on $\Omega\coloneqq{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . Define the following process $\widehat{\sigma}^{2}$ , taking values in ${\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ , which coincides with the density (with respect to the Lebesgue measure) of the quadratic variation of $X$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}\coloneqq\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\dfrac{[X]_{t}-[X]_{t-\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon},\;t\in[0,T]. $$

Given a control process $\beta$ chosen by the agent, taking values in $B$ a subset of some Polish space, the controlled state equation is defined by the following SDE, driven by an $n$ -dimensional Brownian motion $W$ for fixed $n\in\mathbb{N}^{\star}$

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}(X_{\cdot\wedge s},\beta_{s})\big(\lambda_{s}(X_{\cdot\wedge s},\beta_{s})\mathrm{d}s+\mathrm{d}W_{s}\big),\;t\in[0,T], $$

where $\lambda:[0,T]\times\Omega\times B\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\sigma:[0,T]\times\Omega\times B\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d,n}$ are two bounded functions such that, for any $b\in B$ , the map $[0,T]\times\Omega\ni(t,x)\longmapsto(\lambda_{t}(x,b),\sigma_{t}(x,b))\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{d,n}$ is $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable. When convenient, we will denote by $\mu(t,x,b)\coloneqq\sigma_{t}(x,b)\lambda_{t}(x,b)$ , $(t,x,b)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times B$ , the drift coefficient of the output process.

Admissible controls are then defined as $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable processes, taking values in $B$ , and ensuring existence of a weak solution to the above SDE. We refer to [8] for precise details, and note whenever we follow the approach developed in [5], we will additionally require weak uniqueness. In short, we let ${\cal B}$ be the set of admissible controls for the agent, and ${\cal P}$ the corresponding set of admissible probability measures such that, for every $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ , we can find an $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable, $B$ -valued process $\beta^{\mathbb{P}}$ , and an $n$ -dimensional $\mathbb{P}$ –Brownian motion $W^{\mathbb{P}}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle X_{t}=x+\int_{0}^{t}\mu_{s}(X_{\cdot\wedge s},\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s})\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}(X_{\cdot\wedge s},\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s})\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}}_{s},\;t\in[0,T]. $$

Given a terminal payment $\xi\in\mathbb{L}^{0}(\mathbb{R},{\cal F}_{\text{$T$}})$ , namely an $\mathbb{R}$ -valued and ${\cal F}_{\text{$T$}}$ -measurable random variable, the optimisation problem faced by the agent is defined by

$$ \displaystyle V_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi)\coloneqq\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P}),\;\text{with}\;J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[{\cal K}_{\text{$T$}}^{\mathbb{P}}U(\xi)-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}{\cal K}_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}c_{s}\big(\beta_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg],\;\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}, $$

where

- $(i)$ the Borel-measurable utility function $U:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is invertible, and we will denote by $U^{(\text{$-$}1)}$ its inverse;

- $(ii)$ the Borel-measurable cost function $c:[0,T]\times{\cal C}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})\times B\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is such that, for any $b\in B$ , the map $[0,T]\times\Omega\ni(t,x)\longmapsto c_{t}(x,b)\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable, and satisfies the following integrability condition $\displaystyle\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\big|c_{s}\big(\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{s}\big)\big|^{p}\mathrm{d}s\bigg]<+\infty,\;\text{for some}\;p>1;$ (2.4)

- $(iii)$ the discount factor ${\cal K}^{\mathbb{P}}$ is defined for all $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ by

$$ {\cal K}_{t}^{\mathbb{P}}\coloneqq\exp\bigg(-\int_{0}^{t}k_{s}\big(\beta_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg),\;t\in[0,T], $$

where $k:[0,T]\times\Omega\times B\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is assumed to be Borel-measurable, bounded, and such that for any $b\in B$ , the map $[0,T]\times\Omega\ni(t,x)\longmapsto k_{t}(x,b)\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable.

To ensure that the agent’s problem (2.3) is well-defined, we require minimal integrability on the contracts as in [8, Equation (2.5)], but adapted here to our setting with utility function, namely

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\Big[\big|U(\xi)\big|^{p}\Big]<+\infty,\;\text{for some}\;p>1. {\rm I}^{p}_{\text{$\rm A$}} $$

In addition, we assume as usual that the agent has a reservation utility level $R_{\text{$\rm A$}}\in\mathbb{R}$ , which conditions his acceptance of the contract. With this in mind, we consider the following set $\Xi$ of admissible contracts

$$ \displaystyle\Xi\coloneqq\big\{\xi\in\mathbb{L}^{0}(\mathbb{R},{\cal F}_{\text{$T$}}):\text{$\xi$ satisfies \eqref{eq:integrability_contract_agent} and}\;V_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi)\geq R_{\text{$\rm A$}}\big\}. $$

Finally, we denote by ${\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)$ the set of optimal responses of the agent to a contract $\xi\in\Xi$ , i.e.

$$ \displaystyle{\cal P}^{\star}(\xi)\coloneqq\big\{\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}:V_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi)=J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star})\big\}. $$

Subsequently, the principal’s optimisation problem is defined as follows

$$ \displaystyle V_{\text{$\rm P$}}\coloneqq\sup_{\xi\in\Xi}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}\in{\cal P}^{\text{$\star$}}(\xi)}J_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P}^{\star}),\;\text{with}\; \displaystyle J_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[{\cal K}^{\text{$\rm P$},\mathbb{P}}_{\text{$T$}}U_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi)-\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}{\cal K}^{\text{$\rm P$},\mathbb{P}}_{s}c_{s}^{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(\beta_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg],\;\xi\in\Xi,\;\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}, $$

where

- $(i)$ $U_{\text{$\rm P$}}:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a Borel-measurable utility function;

- $(ii)$ $c^{\text{$\rm P$}}:[0,T]\times\Omega\times B\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is Borel-measurable, and the map $[0,T]\times\Omega\ni(t,x)\longmapsto c_{t}^{\text{$\rm P$}}(x,b)\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable for any $b\in B$ ;

- $(iii)$ the discount factor ${\cal K}^{\text{$\rm P$},\mathbb{P}}$ is defined for all $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ by

$$ {\cal K}^{\text{$\rm P$},\mathbb{P}}_{t}\coloneqq\exp\bigg(-\int_{0}^{t}k_{s}^{\text{$\rm P$}}\big(\beta_{s}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg),\;t\in[0,T], $$

where $k^{\text{$\rm P$}}:[0,T]\times\Omega\times B\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is assumed to be Borel-measurable, bounded, and such that for any $b\in B$ , the map $[0,T]\times\Omega\ni(t,x)\longmapsto k^{\text{$\rm P$}}_{t}(x,b)\in\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathbb{F}$ –progressively measurable.

Note that, as is customary in principal–agent problems, if there is more than one optimal response for the agent to a given contract, we assume that the principal selects the one that is most favourable to her. This is consistent with the original economic setting considered historically in principal–agent problems, in which the principal suggests an effort when offering the contract, and the agent simply verifies that this effort is indeed optimal for him. Moreover, since by convention the supremum over an empty set is taken to be minus infinity, the principal should always choose a contract such that a best response exists (unless no such contract exists, which leads to a very degenerate problem, and is thus a situation we ignore).

#### Remark 2.1.

A straightforward generalisation of the above model would allow

$(i)$ the agent’s utility function $U$ to depend on the path of the output process $X_{\cdot\wedge\text{$T$}}$ . No further technical difficulty arises in this case, only invertibility with respect to the $\xi$ -variable should be required;

$(ii)$ the principal to have her own control process $\alpha\in{\cal A}$ , namely an $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable $A$ -valued process, for some subset $A$ of a Polish space. This control may represent, for example, inter-temporal payments to the agent, or efforts that the principal herself can exert on the output process $X$ , and can appear in all the above defined maps. The contract should then be understood as the pair $(\alpha,\xi)$ , meaning that the principal also announces her control at the beginning of the contracting period, see for example Hernández, Hernández Santibáñez, Hubert, and Possamaï (2026) [12]. This modification mainly leads to more cumbersome notations, but no additional technical difficulty.

### 2.2 Previous results

As already mentioned in the introduction, there exist two approaches to solve principal–agent problems with volatility control. In this section, we briefly describe these two methods, which will later be used to introduce a new form of contracts and verify its optimality. For both approaches in [8, 5], we first define the sets of attainable squared diffusion coefficients and corresponding constrained controls, for $(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\Omega$

$$ \displaystyle{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)\coloneqq\big\{[\sigma\sigma^{\top}]_{t}(x,b)\in{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R}):b\in B\big\},\text{ and }B_{t}(x,S)\coloneqq\big\{b\in B:[\sigma\sigma^{\top}]_{t}(x,b)=S\big\},\;S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x). $$

We then introduce, for any $(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ , the agent’s Hamiltonian

$$ \displaystyle H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)\coloneqq\sup_{b\in\text{$B$}}h_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,b),\;\text{with}\;h_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,b)\coloneqq f_{t}(x,y,z,b)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\big[\gamma[\sigma\sigma^{\top}]_{t}(x,b)\big],\;b\in B, $$

as well as its ‘constrained’ version to a specific attainable diffusion $S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$

$$ \displaystyle F_{t}(x,y,z,S) \displaystyle\coloneqq\sup_{b\in\text{$B$}_{\text{$t$}}(x,\text{$S$})}f_{t}(x,y,z,b),\;\mbox{with}\;f_{t}(x,y,z,b)\coloneqq\mu_{t}(x,b)\cdot z-c_{t}(x,b)-k_{t}(x,b)y,\;b\in B. $$

We note the following relationship between $H$ and $F$ , namely that $2H$ is the Fenchel conjugate of $-2F$ ,

$$ \displaystyle H_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)=\sup_{\text{$S$}\in\text{${\bf\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\bigg\{F_{t}(x,y,z,S)+\dfrac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}[S\gamma]\bigg\}. $$

#### 2.2.1 The original approach

Following the approach in [8], we are led to consider terminal payments of the form $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}\big(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}\big)$ , where the process $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}$ is defined as the solution to the following SDE

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}H_{s}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}_{s},Z_{s},\Gamma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}+\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}{\rm Tr}\big[\Gamma_{s}\mathrm{d}[X]_{s}\big],\;\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\;\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}, $$

for a constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and a pair $(Z,\Gamma)$ of processes satisfying appropriate integrability conditions. More precisely, for any $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable, $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ -valued process $Z$ and any $\mathbb{F}$ -adapted, càdlàg, $\mathbb{R}$ -valued process $Y$ , we consider the norms

$$ \displaystyle\|Z\|^{p}_{\mathbb{H}^{\text{$p$}}}\coloneqq\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}Z_{t}^{\top}\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}Z_{t}\mathrm{d}t\bigg)^{p/2}\Bigg],\;\|Y\|^{p}_{\mathbb{D}^{\text{$p$}}}\coloneqq\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,\text{$T$}]}\big|Y_{t}\big|^{p}\bigg]. $$

We can then define the set ${\cal V}$ of appropriate processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ as in [8, Definition 3.2], recalled below.

#### Definition 2.2.

Let $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ . For any $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ , define the process $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}$ using (2.11). We will write $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}$ if moreover

- $(i)$ $\|Z\|_{\mathbb{H}^{\text{$p$}}}<\infty$ and $\|Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}\|_{\mathbb{D}^{\text{$p$}}}<\infty$ for some $p>1;$

- $(ii)$ there exists $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ such that $H_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t}\big)=h_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}\big),\;\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}\text{\rm--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega$ .

It is straightforward to show that any $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}\big(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$}}\big)$ , with $(y_{0},Z,\Gamma)\in\mathbb{R}\times{\cal V}$ , is admissible (see [8, Proposition 3.3]), and that the agent’s optimal response can be characterised as the maximisers of $H$ ; but the proof of [8, Theorem 3.6] may fail if the following assumption is not satisfied (see Remark 3.9), as shown in [5].

#### Assumption 2.3.

There exists a Borel-measurable function $\gamma^{\star}:[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\longrightarrow{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})$ such that for all $(t,\vartheta)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ , we have $F_{t}(\vartheta,S)=H_{t}(\vartheta,\gamma_{t}^{\star}(\vartheta,S))-\frac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}[\gamma_{t}^{\star}(\vartheta,S)S].$

#### 2.2.2 The alternative approach

The approach recently developed in [5] consists in letting the principal directly controls the density of the quadratic variation, in addition to choosing a terminal payment. More precisely, let

$$ \displaystyle{\cal S}\coloneqq\big\{\Sigma:[0,T]\times\Omega\longrightarrow{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R}):\Sigma\;\text{is}\;\mathbb{F}\text{--progressively measurable}\big\}. $$

For fixed $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the agent’s admissible efforts are now limited to those that achieve the desired quadratic variation.

$$ \displaystyle{\cal B}^{\circ}(\Sigma,\mathbb{P}) \displaystyle\coloneqq\big\{\beta\in{\cal B}:\beta_{t}\in B_{t}(\Sigma_{t}),\;\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}\text{\rm--a.e.}\big\},\;\text{and}\;{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)\coloneqq\big\{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}:[\sigma\sigma^{\top}]_{t}(\beta_{t}^{\mathbb{P}})=\Sigma_{t},\;\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}\text{--a.e.}\big\}. $$

As already mentioned, for this approach we actually need to restrict the set of admissible controls to those inducing a unique weak solution to the original SDE (2.1). We refer to [5, Assumption 2.2] and related remarks for a rigorous statement and further justifications. Given $\xi\in\mathbb{L}^{0}({\cal F}_{\text{$T$}},\mathbb{R})$ and $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ , the optimisation problem faced by the agent is

$$ \displaystyle V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\Sigma)\coloneqq\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\text{$\circ$}}(\text{$\Sigma$})}J_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P}). $$

In parallel to (2.5) and (2.6), we define the set $\Xi^{\circ}$ of admissible contracts as

$$ \displaystyle\Xi^{\circ}\coloneqq\big\{(\xi,\Sigma)\in\mathbb{L}^{0}({\cal F}_{\text{$T$}},\mathbb{R})\times{\cal S}:\text{$\xi$ satisfies \eqref{eq:integrability_contract_agent} and}\;V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi,\Sigma)\geq R_{\text{$\rm A$}}\big\}, $$

and denote by ${\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(\xi,\Sigma)$ the set of agent’s optimal response to a contract, here a pair $(\xi,\Sigma)\in\Xi^{\circ}$ . Then, the goal of the principal is to maximise her objective function by choosing $(\xi,\Sigma)\in\Xi^{\circ}$ , anticipating the agent’s optimal response

$$ \displaystyle V_{\text{$\rm P$}}^{\circ}\coloneqq\sup_{(\xi,\text{$\Sigma$})\in\text{$\Xi$}^{\circ}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\text{$\circ$}\text{$,$}\text{$\star$}}(\xi,\text{$\Sigma$})}J_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi,\mathbb{P}). $$

This auxiliary problem is not meant to be economically realistic; rather, it is introduced as a tractable benchmark: its value is easier to characterise than that of the original problem, and we then show that the two values coincide. More precisely, it is first proved in [5, Lemma 3.5] that $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}^{\circ}\geq V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ , namely $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}^{\circ}$ defined above is the best possible value for the principal, if achievable. Then, the above problem can be solved using BSDEs. Indeed, for this alternative problem, [5, Theorem 3.10] states that considering terminal payments of the form $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ})$ , with

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}F_{s}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ}_{s},Z_{s},\Sigma_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\;\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\;\text{for all}\;\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma), $$

is without loss of generality from the principal’s point of view.

#### Definition 2.4.

Let $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ . For any $\Sigma\in{\cal S}$ and any $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable processes $Z$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , define the process $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ}$ using (2.15). We will denote $(Z,\Sigma)\in{\cal V}^{\circ}$ if moreover

- $(i)$ $\|Z\|^{p}_{\mathbb{H}^{\text{$p$}}}<\infty$ and $\|Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ}\|^{p}_{\mathbb{D}^{\text{$p$}}}<\infty$ for some $p>1;$

- $(ii)$ there exists $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\circ}(\Sigma)$ such that $F_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ},Z_{t},\Sigma_{t}\big)=f_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ},Z_{t},\beta_{t}^{\mathbb{P}}\big)$ , $\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}$ –a.e. on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ .

Then, [5, Proposition 3.9] establishes that the agent’s optimal response to such contract $(\xi,\Sigma)$ is given by a maximiser of the constrained Hamiltonian. More precisely, the agent’s optimal effort can be represented by $\mathfrak{b}^{\circ}_{\cdot}\coloneqq b^{\circ}_{\cdot}(Y_{\cdot}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ},Z_{\cdot},\Sigma_{\cdot})$ , where the function $b^{\circ}$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle b^{\circ}_{t}(x,y,z,S)\in\argmax_{b\in\text{$B$}_{\text{$t$}}(x,\text{$S$})}f_{t}(x,y,z,b),\;(t,x,y,z,S)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R}). $$

We further define ${\cal P}^{\circ,\star}(Z,\Sigma)\coloneqq{\cal P}^{\circ,\star}\big(U^{(\text{$-$}1)}\big(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ}\big),\Sigma\big).$ To summarise, we obtained

$$ \displaystyle V_{\text{$\rm P$}}^{\circ}=\sup_{y_{\text{$0$}}\geq\text{$R$}_{\text{$\rm A$}}}\sup_{(\text{$Z$},\text{$\Sigma$})\in{\cal V}^{\circ}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\text{$\circ$}\text{$,$}\text{$\star$}}(\text{$Z$},\text{$\Sigma$})}J_{\text{$\rm P$}}\Big(U^{(\text{$-$}1)}\big(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\circ}\big),\mathbb{P}\Big). $$

More importantly, [5, Theorem 3.12] proves that this value can be achieved using contracts of the form (2.11), under Assumption 2.3. Subsequently, this provides an alternative BSDE-based approach to prove optimality of the contract form (2.11). However, since the two aforementioned approaches may fail when Assumption 2.3 is not satisfied, it is crucial to investigate the existence of optimal contracts beyond this setting. This is the goal of next section.

## 3 General optimal contracts

We first use the 2BSDE characterisation of the agent’s continuation utility to introduce a general form of contracts. We then derive appropriate conditions ensuring that the contract form is revealing for the agent and without loss of generality for the principal. These results are given in Proposition 3.3 and Theorem 3.7. The proof of Proposition 3.3 follows classical arguments, but is included here for the sake of completeness. The proof of Theorem 3.7 relies on both approaches briefly described in the previous sections, and is detailed in Sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 respectively.

### 3.1 Deriving a general form of contracts

As established in [8, Proposition 4.6], for a fixed contract $\xi\in\Xi$ in the original problem, the agent’s continuation utility $Y$ is the first component of the solution $(Y,Z,K)$ to the 2BSDE

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}={U}(\xi)+\int_{t}^{T}F_{s}\big(Y_{s},Z_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s-\int_{t}^{T}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s}+\int_{t}^{T}\mathrm{d}K_{s},\;\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\;\text{for all}\;\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}, $$

where $K$ is a non-decreasing process starting from $K_{0}=0$ , see [8, Definition 4.4]. Adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 3.6 in [8, Section 4.6], as detailed later in Section 3.3.1 for completeness, we can assume without loss of generality that the non-decreasing process $K$ in the 2BSDE is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, with non-negative density denoted $\dot{K}$ . This leads to $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}(Y_{\text{$T$}})$ for the terminal payment, with

$$ \displaystyle Y_{t}=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\big(F_{s}\big(Y_{s},Z_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)+\dot{K}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\;t\in[0,T],\;\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\;\text{for all}\;\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}. $$

From there, the idea is to find a suitable representation for the density $\dot{K}$ , leading to a family of parametric contracts $(\xi^{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ , or an appropriate parameter set $\Theta$ such that each contract $\xi^{\theta}$ is

- $({\cal R})$ revealing, in the sense that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ , $\xi^{\theta}$ is admissible, $V_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi^{\theta})=y_{0}\geq R_{\text{$A$}}$ , and there exists a process $\mathfrak{b}^{\star,\theta}\in{\cal B}$ , depending on $\theta$ and the observable states, such that the optimal responses of the agent are exactly the $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}$ satisfying $\beta^{\mathbb{P}^{\star}}_{t}=\mathfrak{b}^{\star,\theta}_{t}$ , $\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}^{\star}$ –a.e.;

- $({\cal W})$ without loss of generality from the principal’s point of view, in the sense that restricting her optimisation to the sub-family $\{\xi^{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta}\subseteq\Xi$ leaves her value unchanged, namely $\displaystyle V_{\text{$\rm P$}}=\sup_{\theta\in\text{$\Theta$}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}\in{\cal P}^{\text{$\star$}}(\xi^{\text{$\theta$}})}J_{\text{$\rm P$}}(\xi^{\theta},\mathbb{P}^{\star}).$

We will see below that we can take the parameter of the form $\theta=(y_{0},Z,\Gamma,\psi)$ , where $\psi$ belongs to the class $\Psi$ of Definition 3.6: it satisfies Condition C ℛ , ensuring property $({\cal R})$ (see Proposition 3.3), together with Condition C min 𝒲 and either ( a ) or ( b ) of that definition, ensuring property $({\cal W})$ (see Theorem 3.7).

First, in order for the contract to be implementable, the process $\dot{K}$ can only depend on what is observable by the principal. We thus assume

$$ \displaystyle\dot{K}_{t}=\psi_{t}\big(Y_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big)-F_{t}\big(Y_{t},Z_{t},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big),\;t\in[0,T], $$

for some function $\psi:[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , where $E$ is an arbitrary space. Similarly to (2.11) and Definition 2.2, we consider the process $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}$ , defined as a solution to the following SDE for $t\in[0,T]$

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},Z,\Gamma,\psi}_{t}&=y_{0}-\int_{0}^{t}\psi_{s}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{s},Z_{s},\Gamma_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}Z_{s}\cdot\mathrm{d}X_{s},\;\mathbb{P}\textnormal{--a.s.},\end{split} $$

for a constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and a pair $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}^{\psi}$ defined below. To ensure that the above SDE has a unique strong solution, we will further require that the function $\psi$ is Lipschitz-continuous in the $y$ -variable, uniformly in the others, and denote by ${\cal O}$ the set of such Borel-measurable functions $\psi:[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E\times{\cal S}^{\text{$+$}}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ .

#### Definition 3.1.

Let $\psi\in{\cal O}$ and $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ . For any $\mathbb{F}$ -predictable processes $(Z,\Gamma)$ taking values in $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E$ , define the process $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}$ using (3.4). We will write $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}^{\psi}$ if moreover

- $(i)$ for some $p>1$ , $\|Z\|_{\mathbb{H}^{\text{$p$}}}<\infty$ , $\|Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}\|_{\mathbb{D}^{\text{$p$}}}<\infty$ and $\displaystyle\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{\text{$T$}}\psi_{s}\big(0,Z_{s},\Gamma_{s},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{s}\big)\mathrm{d}s\bigg)^{p}\Bigg]<+\infty;$

- $(ii)$ there exists $\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}$ such that $\displaystyle\psi_{t}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big)=F_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi},Z_{t},\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}\big)=f_{t}\big(Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi},Z_{t},\beta^{\mathbb{P}}_{t}\big),\;\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}\text{\rm--a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega.$ (3.5)

Overall, we will consider the following class of contracts.

#### Definition 3.2 (Relevant class of contracts).

A contract $\xi$ belongs to the class of relevant contracts, denoted ${\cal C}$ , if there exist a function $\psi\in{\cal O}$ , a constant $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ and a pair of processes $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}^{\psi}$ such that $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi})$ , for $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}$ defined as in (3.4). We denote by ${\cal P}_{\psi}^{\star}(Z,\Gamma)$ the set of agent’s best response to such contract.

### 3.2 Main results

Given a relevant contract $\xi\in{\cal C}$ as defined above, thus parametrised by a function $\psi\in{\cal O}$ , a constant $y\geq R_{\text{$\rm A$}}$ , and a pair $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}^{\psi}$ , one can show that if the function $\psi$ satisfies in addition Condition C ℛ below, then the contract $\xi$ is admissible and one can easily compute the agent’s optimal response, so that the revealing property $({\cal R})$ is satisfied.

#### Proposition 3.3 (Agent’s optimal response).

Let $\psi\in{\cal O}$ , $y_{0}\geq R_{\text{$\rm A$}}$ and $(Z,\Gamma)\in{\cal V}^{\psi}$ , and consider the associated contract $\xi\in{\cal C}$ , in the sense of Definition 3.2. If the map $\psi$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{\text{$S$}\in\text{${\bf\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\big\{\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\big\}=0,\;\text{\rm for all}\;(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E, {\rm C}_{\text{${\cal R}$}} $$

then $\xi\in\Xi$ , $V_{\text{$\rm A$}}(\xi)=y_{0}\geq R_{\text{$\rm A$}}$ , and all agent’s optimal responses take the form $\mathfrak{b}^{\star,\psi}_{\cdot}\coloneqq b^{\star,\psi}_{\cdot}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{\cdot},Z_{\cdot},\Gamma_{\cdot})$ , where $b^{\star,\psi}$ satisfies for all $(t,x,y,z,\gamma)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times E$

$$ \displaystyle b^{\star,\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)\in\argmax_{b\in\text{$B$}_{\text{$t$}}(x,\text{$S$}^{\text{$\star$}\text{$,$}\text{$\psi$}}_{\text{$t$}}(x,y,z,\gamma))}f_{t}(x,y,z,b),\;S^{\star,\psi}_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma)\in\argmin_{\text{$S$}\in\text{${\bf\Sigma}$}_{\text{$t$}}(x)}\big\{\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\big\}. $$

For later reference, we call $\mathfrak{B}^{\star,\psi}$ the set of all such functions $b^{\star,\psi}$ .

The previous result echoes [8, Proposition 3.3] for the contract form (2.11) and [5, Proposition 3.9] for (2.15). The proof follows standard arguments and is therefore postponed to Appendix A.

#### Remark 3.4.

We note that if the map $\psi$ is taken to be identically equal to $F$ , the maximisation (A.1) boils down to the maximisation over $S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ of the following quantity $\sup_{b\in\text{$B$}_{\text{$t$}}(x,\text{$S$})}\big\{f_{t}(x,y,z,b)\big\}-F_{t}(x,y,z,S),$ which is always $0$ by definition of $F$ . In other words, when taking $\psi\equiv F$ in the contract, the agent is actually indifferent between any achievable quadratic variations. In the end, we will note in Remark 3.12 that since the principal can choose among the agent’s optimal responses, she will be able to select any desired achievable quadratic variation.

The next task is to ensure that the contract form introduced through (3.4) satisfies Property $({\cal W})$ . More precisely, for a fixed parametrisation function $\psi\in{\cal O}$ satisfying Condition C ℛ , the principal’s value function is given by

$$ \displaystyle\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}\coloneqq\sup_{y_{\text{$0$}}\geq R_{\text{$\rm A$}}}\widetilde{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}(y_{0}),\;\text{\rm with}\;\widetilde{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}(y_{0})\coloneqq\sup_{(\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$})\in\text{${\cal V}$}^{\text{$\psi$}}}\sup_{\mathbb{P}\in{\cal P}^{\text{$\star$}}_{\text{$\psi$}}(\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$})}J_{\text{$\rm P$}}\Big(U^{(\text{$-$}1)}\big(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}\big),\mathbb{P}\Big). $$

As proved in Proposition 3.3, any contract $\xi\in{\cal C}$ belongs to the original set of admissible contracts $\Xi$ , thus ensuring that for all $\psi\in{\cal O}$ , the value $\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ defined above is lower than the value $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ . Moreover, under weak uniqueness, it has been noticed in [5, Lemma 3.5] that the latter is smaller than the contractible-volatility value, hence $V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm P$}}\geq V_{\text{$\rm P$}}\geq\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ . While [5] proves that the equalities hold under Assumption 2.3, using the contract form originating from [8], one can actually prove that this result extends beyond this assumption, using two complementary approaches.

The first approach leverages the 2BSDE-based narrative developed in [8] and briefly recalled in Section 2.2.1. In particular, one needs there to ensure that any non-negative density process $\dot{K}$ in (3.2) can be represented using a function $\psi$ as described in (3.3). In other words, the map $E\ni\gamma\longmapsto\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)-F_{t}(x,y,z,S)\in\mathbb{R}$ needs to be surjective onto $[0,+\infty)$ . It is sufficient to assume the above map is continuous and that $\psi$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\gamma\in\text{$E$}}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=F_{t}(x,y,z,S), {\rm C}^{\rm min}_{\text{${\cal W}$}} \displaystyle\sup_{\gamma\in\text{$E$}}\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma,S)=+\infty, {\rm C}^{\rm sup}_{\text{${\cal W}$}} $$

for all $(t,x,y,z)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$ . With the above requirements on $\psi$ , one can follow the 2BSDE approach to show that the value $\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ defined in (3.7) achieves the original value $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ .

Alternatively, one can use the BSDE-based approach, proposed in [5] and summarised in Section 2.2.2. As already mentioned, this approach has the drawback that it requires to assume weak uniqueness for the SDE (2.1). Nonetheless, one can show that if the parametrisation function $\psi\in{\cal O}$ satisfies Condition C ℛ , Condition C min 𝒲 and some additional regularity conditions detailed in Condition 3.5, the associated contract can be proved to be optimal. Although Condition 3.5 may be cumbersome to verify for an arbitrary $\psi\in{\cal O}$ , it suffices to note that $\psi\equiv F$ works.

#### Condition 3.5.

Let $\psi\in{\cal O}$ satisfying Condition C min 𝒲 , and define for $(t,x,y,z)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , $S\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)$

$$ \displaystyle\gamma^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S)\in\argmin_{\gamma\in\text{$E$}}\psi_{t}\big(x,y,z,\gamma,S\big). $$

The map $\psi\circ\gamma^{\star}:(t,x,y,z,S,S^{\prime})\longmapsto\psi_{t}(x,y,z,\gamma_{t}^{\star}(x,y,z,S),S^{\prime})$ is Lipschitz-continuous in $y$ and has linear growth in $z$ , namely there exist $L>0$ and $C>0$ such that for all $(t,x,y,y^{\prime},z)\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $(S,S^{\prime})\in{\bf\Sigma}_{t}(x)^{2}$

$$ \displaystyle\big|\psi_{t}\circ\gamma^{\star}_{t}(x,y,z,S,S^{\prime})-\psi_{t}\circ\gamma_{t}^{\star}(x,y^{\prime},z,S,S^{\prime})\big|\leq L\left|y-y^{\prime}\right|,\;\text{\rm and}\;\left|\psi_{t}\circ\gamma_{t}^{\star}(x,0,z,S,S^{\prime})\right|\leq C\big(1+\|x\|+\|z^{\top}S^{\prime}z\|^{1/2}\big). $$

#### Definition 3.6 (Relevant parametrisation functions).

We let $\Psi$ be the subset of continuous functions $\psi\in{\cal O}$ satisfying Conditions C ℛ and C min 𝒲 , and such that either

- $(a)$ Condition C sup 𝒲 is satisfied;

- $(b)$ or Condition 3.5 holds.

The following theorem states the main results regarding the optimal form of contracts and the equality of the values.

#### Theorem 3.7.

Let $\psi\in\Psi$ , then the contract form parametrised by $\psi$ is optimal. More precisely

- $(i)$ if $\psi$ satisfies ( a ) , $\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}=V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ ;

- $(ii)$ if $\psi$ satisfies ( b ) and weak uniqueness is assumed for SDE (2.1), $\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}=V^{\circ}_{\text{$\rm P$}}=V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ .

Before turning to the proofs, some remarks are in order. First, for fixed $y_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ , the value $\widetilde{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}(y_{0})$ now corresponds to the value of a more standard stochastic control problem. It admits two state variables, $X$ and $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}$ , whose dynamics are respectively given by (2.1) and (3.4), indirectly controlled by the principal through the agent’s best response to a terminal payment $\xi=U^{(\text{$-$}1)}\big(Y_{\text{$T$}}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}\big)$ . More precisely, for an optimal response $\mathfrak{b}^{\star,\psi}_{t}\coloneqq b^{\star,\psi}_{t}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})$ , $\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}^{\star}$ –a.e., characterised via (3.6) and a corresponding probability measure $\mathbb{P}^{\star}\in{\cal P}^{\star}_{\psi}(Z,\Gamma)$ , the pair $(X,Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi})$ is a solution to the following system of controlled SDEs

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\mu_{t}\big(b^{\star,\psi}_{t}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\big(b_{t}^{\star,\psi}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}_{t}, \displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}=\big(c_{t}+Y_{t}^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}k_{t}\big)\big(b^{\star,\psi}_{t}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}t+Z_{t}^{\top}\sigma_{t}\big(b^{\star,\psi}_{t}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big)\mathrm{d}W^{\mathbb{P}^{\text{$\star$}}}_{t}, $$

for $t\in[0,T]$ , with initial condition $X_{0}=x_{0}$ and $Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{0}=y_{0}$ . Indeed, by computing the dynamics (3.4) under the agent’s optimal effort $\mathfrak{b}^{\star}$ , one can notice that by Condition C ℛ and the characterisation (3.6), we have

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{t}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t},S^{\star,\psi}_{t}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big) \displaystyle=F_{t}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},S_{t}^{\star,\psi}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big) \displaystyle=f_{t}\big(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},b_{t}^{\star,\psi}(Y^{y_{\text{$0$}},\text{$Z$},\text{$\Gamma$},\psi}_{t},Z_{t},\Gamma_{t})\big),\;\mathrm{d}t\otimes\mathbb{P}^{\star}\text{\rm--a.e.} $$

One should notice that the function $\psi$ does not explicitly appear in the above SDE system. Indeed, the principal’s value is computed under the agent’s optimal effort, so any chosen parametrisation function $\psi$ vanishes to $F$ , according to Condition C ℛ . However, the optimal effort characterised through the function $b^{\star,\psi}$ does depend on the choice of $\psi$ . Nevertheless, Theorem 3.7 states that the principal’s value $V_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ in the original problem, which is by definition independent of the choice of $\psi$ , is equal to $\overline{V}^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}$ , implying that such value is also be independent of $\psi$ . This will appear more clearly in the proof of the theorem detailed below, but intuitively, one can switch from $\psi\in\Psi$ to another $\phi\in\Psi$ using the fact that they should both satisfy Conditions C ℛ and C min 𝒲 .

To completely solve the principal’s problem, one can then write the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation satisfied by $V^{\psi}_{\text{$\rm P$}}(y_{0})$ introduced in (3.7) and look for an appropriate solution. More precisely, the Hamiltonian functional for the principal’s problem is now given, for any $(t,x,y,v,p_{x},p_{y},q_{xx},q_{yy},q_{xy})\in[0,T]\times\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}\times{\cal S}_{d}(\mathbb{R})\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , by

$$ \displaystyle H_{t}^{\text{$\rm P$}}(x,y,v,p_{x},p_{y},q_{xx},q_{yy},q_{xy})\coloneqq\sup_{(z,\gamma)\in\mathbb{R}^{\text{$d$}}\times\text{$E$}}\sup_{b^{\text{$\star$}\text{$,$}\text{$\psi$}}\in\text{$\mathfrak{B}$}^{\text{$\star$}\text{$,$}\text{$\psi$}}}h_{t}^{\text{$\rm P$}}(x,y,v,p_{x},p_{y},q_{xx},q_{yy},q_{xy},z,\gamma), $$

where
