SR-1815 is a multi-kinase inhibitor The ﬁndings above support a model in which SR-1815 inhibits CLK1/2, reduces SR-protein phosphorylation, and alters splicing in a manner that contributes to increased Syngap1/SynGAP abundance. However, the temporal separation between acute splicing changes and the longer-term Syngap1 poison-exon response, together with the broader neuronal response to SR-1815, suggested that CLK inhibition may contribute to, but not fully explain, the compound’s activity. Consistent with CLK inhibition contributing to SynGAP regulation, TG003, a chemically distinct CLK-family inhibitor, enhanced SynGAP expression, but was less efﬁcacious than SR-1815 (Fig. 6D)58. This partial phenocopy supports CLK involvement while indicating that SR-1815 efﬁcacy is unlikely to be explained by CLK inhibition alone. Because small-molecule kinase inhibitors frequently engage more than one target, we next asked whether SR-1815 acts through a broader kinase target matrix. We screened SR-1815 across a kinome-wide binding panel to deﬁne its kinase engagement proﬁle59. A measure of kinase inhibitor selectivity showed that SR-1815 engaged <8% of the kinome (Fig. 6E and Supplementary Fig. 14A, and Supplementary Data 40), positioning it as a relatively selective multi-kinase inhibitor with similarities to several

FDA-approved cancer therapeutics (Supplementary Fig. 14B). As expected, SR-1815 strongly engaged CLK1/2 in this assay (Fig. 6E and Supplementary Fig. 14A). Additional activity was observed across six kinase families (Supplementary Fig. 14B), with high-afﬁnity targets in the receptor tyrosine kinase family, including KIT, FLT1, FLT3, TrkA/ TrkB, PDGFRβ, and CSF1R. In-cell kinase occupancy proﬁling further conﬁrmed SR-1815 binding to kinases in cells (Supplementary Fig. 14C–F and Supplementary Data 41–44). To determine whether kinase targets beyond CLK1/2 could contribute to SynGAP regulation, we mined several databases to identify small molecules known to inhibit one or more SR-1815 targets and tested their ability to upregulate SynGAP (Fig. 6F, G). Sunitinib exhibited strong activity in the SynGAP expression assay, whereas the other tested inhibitors either had no effect or reduced assay activity (Fig. 6G)60. Whereas these other inhibitors shared at least one highafﬁnity target with SR-1815, only sunitinib shared high-afﬁnity targets across multiple kinase families, including receptor tyrosine kinases, STE-family kinases, and CDK/MAPK/GSK/CLK-family kinases within the CMGC group (Fig. 6F and Supplementary Fig. 14B)61. This pattern suggests that SynGAP upregulation is not explained by inhibition of a single shared target, but instead may require coordinated engagement of multiple kinase pathways. SR-1815 was more efﬁcacious than sunitinib in the SynGAP expression assay (Fig. 6G). This difference is not simply explained by broader kinase engagement, because SR-1815 is more selective than sunitinib (Supplementary Fig. 14B). Instead, the enhanced activity of SR-1815 may reﬂect its distinct target matrix. Among targets that distinguish SR-1815 from sunitinib, TrkA/TrkB were notable. TrkB-Fc, which attenuates TrkB signaling, increased the SynGAP assay signal by ~20% (Fig. 6G). This partial effect suggests that TrkB-related signaling may contribute to SR-1815 efﬁcacy, but, like TG003, does not fully phenocopy SR-1815. Together, these inhibitor-comparison data support a polypharmacological model in which CLK inhibition is a key contributor to SynGAP regulation, while additional SR-1815 kinase targets, potentially including TrkB-related signaling, enhance the full SynGAP expression response. Finally, the SR-1815 target proﬁle, including high-afﬁnity engagement of kinases implicated in cancer biology, suggested that the compound may also show antiproliferative activity in cancer models (Fig. 6F and Supplementary Fig. 14A–B). Consistent with this prediction, SR-1815 exhibited potent antiproliferative effects in cancer cell lines selected based on overlap with its high-afﬁnity kinase targets (Fig. 6H and Supplementary Fig. 15A–E)62,63. These ﬁndings extend the SR-1815 de-orphaning analysis beyond the initial neuronal phenotype and illustrate how mechanistic interpretation of phenotypic hits can reveal biological activity across distinct disease contexts.

Discussion Proximity labeling has become a mainstay method in molecular biology for understanding the interactomes of speciﬁc proteins in a native environment. Our approach provides evidence that PL can be used for unbiased discovery of ligand-induced changes to chromatin occupancy. This application of PL assigns a molecular ﬁngerprint to a speciﬁc cellular stimulus that, in many cases, is more data rich than global analysis of expressed genes. Existing chromatin proteomic and genomic approaches, including chromatin fractionation, ChIP-based methods, ChIP-MS/RIME-style workﬂows, and proximity-labeling strategies, provide powerful but distinct views of chromatin biology. These methods differ in antibody dependence, locus speciﬁcity, labeling radius, temporal resolution, and ability to distinguish

chromatin-proximal redistribution from bulk abundance changes. MesoMap is intended to complement these approaches by providing a rapid, proximity-based readout of stimulus-induced changes in proteins associated with chromatin. Beyond proving the approach is possible, MesoMap provided molecular insights into how chromatin is regulated in response to HDAC inhibition. These mesoscale changes to protein localization can also be combined with other ‘omics techniques to generate mechanistic hypotheses. For example, comparison of phosphopeptides with proteins enriched by MesoMap revealed correlations between localization and phosphorylation of the AP-1 and B-WICH complexes (Supplementary Fig. 10C–G)64,65.

MesoMap also provided a mechanism-prioritization strategy for de-orphaning SR-1815, a phenotypically discovered SynGAP-restoring probe44. In this application, MesoMap detected altered chromatin association of CLK-family kinases and RNA-splicing machinery, prioritizing a kinase/splicing axis that was subsequently supported by ADP- Glo kinase assays, SR-protein phosphorylation changes, neuronal splicing analysis, and inhibitor-comparison experiments. Thus, Meso- Map did not serve as a stand-alone proof of causality. Rather, it provided chromatin-proximal information that helped prioritize candidate mechanisms not apparent from abundance-based proteomics alone. The SR-1815 application also illustrates an important feature of phenotypic probe de-orphaning, where biologically active compounds may produce both proximal target-dependent effects and longer-term adaptive cell-state remodeling. We therefore do not interpret the twoweek neuronal transcriptomic and proteomic changes as exclusively direct consequences of immediate CLK inhibition. Instead, the data

support a staged model in which SR-1815 acutely engages kinase/splicing-associated pathways, while the disease-relevant Syngap1 poisonexon event, SynGAP abundance changes, and functional neuronal effects emerge over a longer remodeling window. In this framework, broad longer-term changes in postsynaptic and neuronal-state pathways should not be interpreted automatically as nonspeciﬁc toxicity. Rather, they require functional validation. Samowitz et al. provide such a validation by showing that SR-1815 restores SynGAP abundance and produces genotype-dependent effects on synaptic and neuronal function in wildtype versus Syngap1 haploinsufﬁcient neurons44. Together, these ﬁndings support a polypharmacological model in which CLK inhibition contributes to SynGAP regulation, while additional SR-1815 kinase targets enhance the full SynGAP expression response. Methods Cell culture HEK 293 T cells were cultured as a monolayer in DMEM (Gibco #11995073), supplemented with 10% v/v FBS (R&D Systems S11150), 100 U mL−1 of penicillin 100 µg mL−1 of streptomycin (Gibco 15140-122). Cells were maintained in an incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Pc293T cells were grown in complete DMEM media (above) with the addition of 400 µg/mL Zeocin (Invitrogen 46-0072) and 100 µg/mL Hygromycin (Invitrogen 10687010).

Stable cell line generation The pACEMAM3 Integrator Module (Geneva Biotech) bearing H2A-HA- CfaN-FLAG, H3.1-HA-CfaN-FLAG, H3.3-HA-CfaN-FLAG, and H4-HA- CfaN-FLAG was linearized using PI-PspI restriction enzyme (New England Biolabs R0695S). DNA was electrophoretically separated through a 1% agarose gel, linearized bands were excised, and DNA was puriﬁed using the Monarch DNA gel extraction kit (New England Biolabs T1020L). 3.5 µg of linearized plasmid was transfected into 60% con- ﬂuent HEK293T cells grown in a 10 cm plate using Lipofectamine 2000 (ThermoFisher Scientiﬁc 11668027) and incubated for 24 h. Cells underwent selection with media containing 100 µg/mL hygromycin (Invitrogen 10687010) and 400 µg/mL Zeocin (Gibco R25001). After recovery, cells underwent FACS performed by the ﬂow cytometry core at The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation and Technology on a BD FACSAria Fusion (BD biosciences). Single cells expressing GFP in top 10% of cell population were plated in single cells per well in a 96-well plate. Colonies were expanded while continuing antibiotic treatment.

Flow cytometry 1×106 cells were collected with trypsin and quenched with complete media. Cells were pelleted at 400 × g for 3 min, supernatant was removed, and cells were washed with DPBS. Cells were pelleted and resuspended in sort buffer (2.5 mM EDTA, 25 mM HEPES pH 7.0, 1% FBS) and passed through 35 µm strainer. Cells were analyzed using a BD LSR II (BD Biosciences) and gated for live cells and singlets using forward and side scatter characteristics and GFP expression was captured using 488 nm laser. A minimum of 10,000 events were captured per sample. GFP signal was gated using wild type HEK293T cells as negative control. FlowJo software was used to analyze data and create ﬁgures.

Transient transfection For single histone construct µMap experiments HEK293T cells grown to 60% conﬂuence in 10 cm plates were transfected with 3.5 µg of plasmid DNA using Lipofectamine 2000 and incubated overnight. Media was changed to complete media and cells were treated with 10 nM romidepsin or DMSO for 24 h and collected. Subsequent labeling and data analysis were conducted as described below for MesoMap experiments.

Western blot Cell lysates were quantiﬁed using Pierce BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Scientiﬁc #A55864) and normalized to same concentration. Samples

were electrophoretically separated with a pre-cast Invitrogen NuPAGE 4-12% bis-tris acrylamide gel (Invitrogen #NW04125BOX) and transferred to nitrocellulose membrane. Samples were then stained with Revert 520 total protein stain (LICOR Bio 926-10011) and imaged on a Licor Odyssey M. The membranes were then blocked with 2% BSA in TBST for 1 h at room temperature and stained with primary antibody diluted in TBST overnight at 4 °C (dilutions based on antibody manufacturer recommendations). Membranes were washed 3x with TBST and then stained with secondary ﬂuorescent antibody diluted 1:10,000 in TBST for 1 h at room temperature (Licor: 926-68070 and 926-32211; Invitrogen: A32787 and A32731). Membranes were then washed 3x with TBST and imaged on Licor Odyssey M. Quantiﬁcation of western blots was performed in Fiji. Uncropped and unprocessed blots are included in the supplementary information and source data ﬁles.

Immunocytochemistry Cells were cultured, plated, ﬁxed and permeabilized as described for proximity ligation assays. Coverslips were then blocked with 1% BSA in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. Coverslips were then incubated with primary antibody diluted 1:200 in 1% BSA in PBS overnight at 4 °C. Samples were then washed 3x with PBS and incubated with secondary antibody diluted 1:1000 for 1 h at room temperature. Slides were then washed 3x with PBS and mounted to slides using Vectashield DAPI mounting media and sealed with clear nail polish. Slides were imaged as described for the proximity ligation assays.

CUT&TAG CUT&Tag was performed using the CUT&Tag-IT® Assay Kit (Active Motif # 53160). The manufacturer protocol was followed with the application of the following antibodies: Histone H3K27me3 (Active Motif #39157), H3K27ac (Active Motif #39134), DYKDDDDK Tag (Epi- Cypher #13-2031), H3.3 (EpiCypher # 13-0061), and Rabbit IgG (Cell Signaling #2729S). pc293T cells per sample. For FLAG and histone H3.3 experiment, spikein normalization was performed using the CUT&Tag-IT Spike-In Control, Anti-Rabbit (Active Motif #53168). Spike-in normalization was performed by aligning reads in parallel to the Drosophila melanogaster reference genome (BDGP6.54, Ensembl release 114) using Bowtie2. Uniquely mapping Drosophila read counts were tallied per sample, and the sample with the lowest Drosophila read count was assigned a normalization factor of 1.0. For all other samples, a normalization factor was computed as (lowest Drosophila count) / (per-sample Drosophila count), and this factor was used to down-sample the corresponding human-aligned reads, following the manufacturer’s recommended workﬂow (Active Motif #53168, CUT&- Tag Normalization Guidelines). Down-sampled human read counts were then used for all downstream peak calling, bigWig generation, and signal quantiﬁcation, as implemented in the nf-core/cutandrun pipeline (v3.2.2). Mitochondrial reads (chromosome preﬁx “MT”) were removed post-alignment using SAMtools (v1.17). Peak calling was conducted with MACS2 (v2.2.7.1) at a q-value threshold of 0.01, incorporating IgG controls scaled by a factor of 0.5 and blacklist ﬁltering using the hg38 blacklist (hg38-blacklist.v2.bed.gz)67. Consensus peaks were generated via BEDTools (v2.31.0) merging. Quality control metrics included fragment length distributions, library complexity estimation with Preseq (v3.1.1), and multi-sample correlations/heatmaps via deepTools (v3.5.1).

MNase-seq Mononucleosome associated DNA was isolated by MNase digestion following the manufacturer’s protocol for the EZ Nucleosomal DNA Prep Kit (Zymo Research # D5220). Digested DNA was separated by electrophoresis on a 2% agarose gel. Mononucleosome DNA bands were excised and puriﬁed using Monarch DNA Gel Extraction Kit (New England Biolabs # T1020). Puriﬁed DNA was submitted to the The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology Genomics Core for library prep and sequencing. Sequencing was conducted on a NextSeq 2000 at >40 m reads per sample. Three bio replicates were run using 1 × 106 cells per replicate of either WT HEK293T or pc293T cells.

MNase-seq data analysis Raw FASTQ reads were processed using the nucMACC in MNaseQC analysis mode, executed under a Singularity container engine68. Quality control was performed on raw reads with FastQC (v 0.11.9), followed by alignment to the human reference genome (GRCh38, Ensembl release 111) using Bowtie2 (v 2.4.4). Post-alignment QC was conducted with Qualimap (2.2.2), including fragment size distribution plotting. Fragments were grouped by size using deepTools (v 3.5.1) alignmentSieve (mono-nucleosome: 140–200 bp; sub-nucleosome: <140 bp), with blacklist ﬁltering applied using the hg38 blacklist (hg38- blacklist.v2.bed.gz)67. Nucleosome positions were called for mono- and sub-nucleosomes using the DANPOS2 (v 2.2.2) dpos algorithm. Additional QC included TSS proﬁles via deepTools computeMatrix, GC content analysis with bedtools genomecov, fragment counting with featureCounts, PCA and correlation analysis with deepTools, and summary reports generated by MultiQC. Aligned BAM ﬁles, including ﬁltered versions, were published for downstream use. The effective genome size was set to 2,721,903,787 (linearly interpolated for 61 bp reads). DANPOS-derived nucleosome maps (in WIG format) were converted to BigWig tracks for visualization in IGV using UCSC wig- ToBigWig (v 2.8).

Proximity labeling For cells treated with compound, all lysis buffers contained compound or vehicle at same concentration as treatment. A total of 3 × 107 cells expressing POI-HA-CfaN-FLAG were resuspended in 1 mL PBS and then lysed with addition of 4 volumes of ice-cold lysis buffer (45 mM KCl, 0.1 mM EDTA, 6.25 mM MgCl2, 12.5 mM Tris, 375 mM Sucrose, 0.125% Nonidep P40, 1x Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail EDTA-free Thermo Scientiﬁc #1861279) for 10 min on ice. The crude nuclei were isolated

by centrifugation at 400xg for 5 min at 4 °C. The nuclei were washed 3x with DPBS + Halt Protease Inhibitor and centrifugation at 400 g for 5 min to pellet nuclei. The nuclei were resuspended in 600 µL of DPBS with 0.25 µM CfaC-Ir or CfaC-biotin. The nuclei were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min with gentle end-over-end rotation. The nuclei were isolated by centrifugation at 400xg for 5 min at 4 °C and washed twice with DPBS (500 µL) to remove excess peptide. The pellets were then resuspended in 1 mL of DPBS containing diazirine–biotin conjugate (200 µM) and irradiated with blue light for 1 min in the Penn PhD Photoreactor M2 at 100% light intensity at 4 °C. The nuclei were re-isolated by centrifugation at 400 × g for 5 min at 4 °C and washed once with DPBS to remove excess biotin–diazirine. The washed pellets were then resuspended in 1 mL of LB3 buffer (10 mM Tris, 100 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM EGTA, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 0.5% sodium lauroyl sarcosinate, pH 7.5) and sonicated using Diagenode Bioruptor Plus for 14 cycles of 30 sec on and 30 sec off at max power and 4 °C.

Streptavidin enrichment The lysed nuclei were then clariﬁed through centrifugation at 15,000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C and the protein concentration of the supernatant was determined by BCA assay. Protein concentration was normalized across all experimental replicates and diluted to 1 mg/mL with LB3. Then 1 mL of each sample was incubated with 125 µL of prewashed magnetic Sepharose streptavidin beads (Cytiva Life Sciences no. 28985738) for 2 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C with end-over-end rotation. The beads were subsequently washed 3x with 1% w/v SDS in PBS, 3x with 1 M NaCl in PBS and 3 × 10% ethyl alcohol in PBS for 5 min each wash with end-over-end rotation.

Label free proximity proteomics Following streptavidin enrichment, the beads were resuspended in PBS (500 µL) and transferred to a new 1.5 mL LoBind tube. The supernatant was removed, and the beads were washed with 3× PBS (0.5 mL) and 3× ammonium bicarbonate (100 mM). The beads were resuspended in 500 µL of 3 M urea in PBS and 25 µL of 200 mM dithiothreitol in 25 mM NH4HCO3 was added. The beads were incubated at 55 °C for 30 min. Subsequently, 30 µL of 500 mM iodoacetamide in 25 mM NH4HCO3 was added and incubated for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. The supernatant was removed and the beads washed with 3x with 0.5 mL of DPBS and 6x with 0.5 mL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate. The beads were resuspended in 0.5 mL of ammonium bicarbonate (50 mM) and transferred to a new protein LoBind tube. The beads were resuspended in 40 µL of ammonium bicarbonate (50 mM), 1.2 µL of trypsin (1 mg/mL in 50 mM acetic acid) was added and the beads incubated overnight with end-over-end rotation at 37 °C. After 16 h, a further 0.8 µL of trypsin was added and the beads were incubated for an extra 1 h at 37 °C. Supernatant was then transferred to new LoBind tubes and each biological replicate split into two technical replicates.

Label free nuclear proteomics After splicing and lysis of nuclei in LB3, 20 µg of protein was taken for cleanup and digestion. Proteins was cleaned up and digested using Sera-Mag Carboxylate SpeedBeads (Cytiva Life Sciences: E7 Cat. #45152105050250 and E3 Cat. #65152105050250) following manufacturer’s protocol. Digested peptides were split into two technical replicates per sample.

Following drying under vacuum, peptides were re-solubilized in 20 µL of 0.1% formic acid (FA) to a ﬁnal concentration of 100 ng/µL. Samples were analyzed on a nanoElute (plug-in V2.1.60.0;

The Bruker TimsTOF Pro 2 was operated in DIA-PASEF mode using Tims Control v. 5.0.2. Settings for the MS method were as follows: Mass Range 100 to 1700 m/z, 1/K0 Start 0.6 V·s/cm2 End 1.4 V·s/ cm2, TIMS Ramp and accumulation time 75 ms, Capillary Voltage 1700 V, Dry Gas 3 L/min, Dry Temp 200 °C, DIA-PASEF settings: 18 MS/ MS scans (50 m/z windows, 0.21 1/K0 windows, total cycle time 0.74), mass range 300 to 1200, and CID collision energy 20 eV (at 0.60, 1/K0) to 65 eV (at 1.60, 1/K0). The analysis was performed at The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology, Mass Spectrometry and Proteomics Core Facility (RRID:SCR_023576). Data was processed via DIANN 1.8.1. Parameters set as follows: trypsin/P digestion, 3 missed cleavages, 3 max. variable modiﬁcations, N-term M excision, Ox(M), Ac(N-term) and C carbamidomethylation. Peptide length range was 7–30, precursor charge range 1-4, m/z range 300-1800, and fragment ion range 200-1800. Mass accuracy and MS accuracy were both set to 10. The following settings on the algorithm were checked: “Use isotopologues”, “MBR”, “No shared spectra”, “Heuristic protein inference”. Precursor FDR was set to 1%. A spectral library was used generated via DIANN from all known human proteins (In-Silico spectral library). The resulting matrix.pg ﬁle was opened in Perseus (v2.0.7.0). Intensities were inputted as “main”, the rest of the descriptors are categorical. Data was then transformed (Log2). Data was log2-transformed and annotated by treatment group. Missing values were imputed using Perseus default settings (random values from a downshifted normal distribution, width = 0.3, shift = 1.8). Normalization was performed via median subtraction. Differential abundance analysis was performed using a two-sample t test with permutation-based FDR correction (250 randomizations, FDR = 0.05, S0 = 0.1) as implemented in Perseus. S0 = 0.1 and 250 randomizations were used as the Perseus defaults for the permutation-based twosample t test, which implements the SAM procedure of Tusher et al. 200169,70. For our group sizes (n = 3 or n = 6 per condition), the full label-permutation space is small (20 distinct partitions for n = 3; 924 for n = 6), so 250 randomizations densely sample the null distribution. Proteins meeting the FDR < 0.05 threshold are considered signiﬁcantly changed. All n = 6 samples represent 3 biological replicates each measured in 2 technical replicates, which were treated as individual observations in statistical testing. The resulting volcano plots were plotted in GraphPad Prism 10 for ﬁnal ﬁgures, following the standard SAM/Perseus convention in which the y-axis displays −log10(p-value) and the curved cutoff demarcates the permutation-based FDR < 0.05 boundary; points called as signiﬁcant are therefore those above the FDR curve, not those above a ﬁxed p-value threshold. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was performed using Metascape with the full human proteome as the background gene set. Enrichment signiﬁcance was assessed using hypergeometric testing with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction as implemented in Metascape’s default parameters71. Panther database was used to identify complex members72.

The supernatant was removed, and the beads were washed with 3× PBS (0.5 ml) and 3× ammonium bicarbonate (100 mM). The beads were resuspended in 500 µl of 3 M urea in PBS and 25 µl of 200 mM dithiothreitol in 25 mM NH4HCO3 was added. The beads were incubated at 55 °C for 30 min. Subsequently, 30 µl of 500 mM iodoacetamide in 25 mM NH4HCO3 was added and incubated for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. The supernatant was removed, and the beads washed 3x with 0.5 ml of DPBS and 6×0.5 ml of 50 mM Triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc #90114). The beads were resuspended in 0.5 ml of TEAB (50 mM) and transferred to a new protein LoBind tube. The beads were resuspended in 40 µl of TEAB (50 mM), 1.2 µl of trypsin (1 mg ml−1 in 50 mM acetic acid) was added and the beads incubated overnight with end-over-end rotation at 37 °C. After 16 h, a further 0.8 µl of trypsin was added and the beads were incubated for an extra 1 h at 37 °C. A total of 20 µl of each TMT reagent was added to the appropriate sample. The reaction was incubated for 2 h at room temperature. The samples were quenched with 8 µl of 5% hydroxylamine and incubated for 15 min. The samples were pooled in a new Protein LoBind tube and acidiﬁed with TFA (16 µl, Optima).

TMT-plex proteomics data analysis Pooled and plexed TMT-labeled samples were ﬁrst dried under vacuum and resolubilized in 400 mL of 1% TFA (pH <3). The mixture was then desalted using Waters Oassis® OASIS HLB 1cc solid phase extraction cartridges (Waters, Milldford, MA), and then dried under vacuum once again. The dried labeled peptide plexed sample was then resuspended in 400uL of 1 M TEAB and fractionated using an Agilent 1100 HPLC system and high pH reversed phase chromatography on a Zorbax Eclipse XDB-C18 column (4.6 × 150 mm, 5-micron) from Agilent (Santa Clara, CA). Sixty fractions were collected at 0.5 mL/min over 105 min using a gradient of 0–5% solvent B in 10 min, 5–35% solvent B in 60 min, 35–70% solvent B in 15 min, a 10 min hold of 70% solvent B, and ﬁnally a return to 5% solvent B in 10 min. Solvent A consisted of 100 mM TEAB and solvent B consisted of ACN. Chromatin fractionation Cells were treated with either DMSO or 10 nM romidepsin for 6 h were harvested by trypsinization and washed twice with ice cold DPBS and centrifugation at 400xg. 1×106 cells per sample were resuspended in 250uL hypotonic lysis buffer (10 mM tris, 15 mM NaCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 1x Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail EDTA-free Thermo Scientiﬁc #1861279) and incubated for 30 min on ice. 12.5ul of 5% NP-40 in H2O was added to samples for ﬁnal concentration of 0.25% and vortexed for 10 sec. Nuclei were isolated by centrifugation at 400 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Supernatant was collected as cytoplasmic fraction. Nuclei resuspended in 500ul of hypotonic lysis buffer supplemented with 1% v/v Triton X-100. Nuclei were lysed with 10 strokes of tight Dounce homogenizer (Active Motif #40401). Samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Supernatant was collected as nucleoplasmic fraction. Remaining chromatin fraction was resuspended in 1x M-PER (ThermoFisher #78501) with 250 U/mL pierce universal nuclease (ThermoFisher #88700). Samples were then sonicated for 10 cycles of 30 sec on and 30 sec off at max power at 4 °C on Diagenode Bioruptor Plus. Samples were centrifuged at 17,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, and supernatant was collected as chromatin fraction. Protein concentration was quantiﬁed using BCA assay (Thermo Scientiﬁc #A55864). 20 µg of protein was taken for cleanup and digestion. Proteins were cleaned up and digested using Sera-Mag Carboxylate SpeedBeads (Cytiva Life Sciences: E7 Cat. #45152105050250 and E3 Cat. #65152105050250) following manufacturer’s protocol. Digested peptides were split into two technical replicates per sample for label free proteomics as described above.

Proximity ligation assay Round coverslips were place in a 12-well plate and washed with 100% ethanol. Wells were then washed with H2O and treated with polylysine (Sigma Aldrich #P4707) for 10 min, followed by two washes with H2O and allowed to airdry for 2 h. Cells were then plated at 2 × 105 cells/well and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were then treated with 10 nM romidepsin or vehicle and incubated for desired time. At the indicated time, the media was aspirated, the wells were washed 2x with DPBS and ﬁxed for 10 min with 4% Formaldehyde in DPBS at room temp. Cells were then washed 2x with DPBS, and permeabilized with pre-chilled 100% MeOH for 5 min at −20 °C. Slides were washed 3x with DPBS. Once ﬁxed and permeabilized proximity ligation was carried out as recommended by manufacturer using the Duolink in situ red starter kit mouse/rabbit (Sigma-Aldrich DUO92101). In brief, slides were blocked

for 1 h at 37 °C with blocking buffer. Slides were then incubated with primary antibodies diluted 1:200 in antibody binding buffer at 4 °C overnight. Slides were washed with wash buffer A and then incubated with PLA probe plus donkey anti-rabbit IgG and PLA probe minus donkey anti-mouse IgG antibodies for 1 h at 37 °C. Samples were washed with wash buffer A and incubated for 30 min at 37 °C with Duolink ligase reaction solution. Slides were washed with wash buffer A and incubated for 100 min with duolink ampliﬁcation solution. Slides were washed with wash buffer B and mounted with duolink in situ mounting media with DAPI and sealed with clear nail polish. Slides were imaged on a Nikon Eclipse Ti2 with a CFI60 Plan Apochromat Lambda D 100x Oil Immersion Objective Lens, N.A. 1.45, W.D. 0.13 mm, F.O.V. 25 mm, DIC, Spring Loaded. Cells located using DAPI channel to eliminate bias for PLA signal. Z-stack images were taken with with DAPI, channel 488, and channel 550 using 0.2 µm z-spacing between 11 total images. At least 5 images were taken of each replicate and quantiﬁed using CellProﬁler nuclear speckle counting software77. Statistical signiﬁcance was determined by a two-tailed unpaired t test of foci per nuclei using Graphpad Prism with outliers excluded (ROUT method with Q = 1%) to limit bias from staining inconsistencies.

Neuronal RNA Seq Neurons were isolated from Syngap1 conditional rescue (Syngap1+/ls) mice and plated using a BioTek EL406 (Agilent Technologies) into 384- well plates pre-coated with poly-D-lysine (PDL) (Aurora ABE2-01200B- PDL) at 15,000 cells in 80 µL/ well and placed in 37 °C incubator80. A solution of 1% agarose was placed in the evaporation border wells prior to plating to minimize edge effects. On DIV 3, 10 µM 5-ﬂuoro-2′-

deoxyuridine ( + FUDR) was added cultures to suppress the proliferation of glia. For 2-week treatments of SR-1815, cultures were treated with vehicle (DMSO) or SR-1815 at 1.5 µM on DIV 0, 3, 7, and 10 by replacing 50% of the conditioned media with fresh feeding media ( + FUDR). For 4 h treatments, 50% of media was replaced with fresh feeding media on DIV 3, 7, and 10. On DIV 14 cultures were supplied vehicle or SR-1815 at 4.4 µM for 4 h through 50% media exchange. On DIV 14 media was removed and 20 µL of DNA/RNA Shield (Zymo: R1100-50) was added to each well. Sample was collected and RNA was extracted using Zymo Quick-RNA MicroPrep kit (Zymo: R1050) following manufacturer protocol. Total RNA was submitted to The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology - Genomics Core (RRID:SCR_017827), where it was quantiﬁed using a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) and evaluated on an Agilent 4200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) for quality assessment. All RNA samples were good quality with RNA Integrity Number (RIN) > 8.0 and were processed for mRNA-seq library preparation. RNase-free working environment was maintained, and RNase-free tips, tubes, and plates were utilized for the subsequent steps. Messenger RNA was selectively isolated from total RNA (300 ng input) using oligo(dT)25 magnetic beads according to the manufacturer’s guidelines in the NEBNext poly(A) mRNA magnetic isolation module (Cat. # E7490, NEB, Ipswich, MA). The library preparation from the enriched mRNA was conducted according to NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA kit (Cat. # E7760, NEB, Ipswich, MA). Brieﬂy, the enriched mRNA samples were chemically fragmented in a buffer containing divalent cations by heating to 94 °C for 15 min. The fragmented RNA was random hexamer primed and reverse transcribed to generate the ﬁrst strand of cDNA. The second strand was synthesized after removing the RNA template and incorporating dUTP in place of dTTP to maintain strand speciﬁcity. Fragmented ds cDNA was then end repaired and adenylated at their 3’ ends. A corresponding ‘T’ nucleotide on the adapters was utilized for ligating the adapter sequences to the cDNA. The adapter ligated DNA was puriﬁed using magnetic beads and PCR ampliﬁed (using 11 cycles) to incorporate a unique barcode and to generate the ﬁnal libraries. The ﬁnal libraries were puriﬁed using magnetic beads to remove any remaining primers and adapters. The ﬁnal libraries were validated on an Agilent 4200 TapeStation (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA), normalized to 4 nM, pooled equally, and loaded onto an Illumina NextSeq 2000 P3 100-cycle ﬂow cell (Cat. # 20040559, Illumina, San Diego, CA) at 750pM ﬁnal concentration and sequenced using 2 x 51 bp paired-end chemistry. On average we generated ~90 million reads pass ﬁlter (base quality score >Q30 suggesting less than 1 error in 1000 bp) per sample for 4 h and 14 day treatment groups.

RNA-seq data analysis Raw FASTQ reads were processed with the publicly available tools and parameters listed below, executed on a SLURM high-performance computing cluster. Quality control was performed on raw reads including adapter trimming and low-quality base removal using Cutadapt (v3.4) with parameters –nextseq-trim=20, --max-n = 0.1 and post trim minimum length set to 32. Reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (ENSEMBL GRCm38.r91) using STAR aligner. Postalignment QC was conducted including contamination screening for rRNA, tRNA, mitochondrial, and mycoplasma sequences using FastQ Screen (v0.14.0). Gene abundance was estimated using HTSeq (v0.11.2) with Python (v3.7.3). Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 with R (v4.2.3), applying regularized log transformation and adjusted p-value correction for multiple testing. Additional QC included PCA analysis, sample-to-sample distance calculations using Euclidean metrics, and heatmap visualization of the

most abundant and differentially expressed genes. Normalized count tables including DESeq2 normalized counts and TPM values were generated for downstream analyzes. Mouse gene names from the DEG list were converted to human equivalents using BioMart on ENSEMBL, since SynGO database only maps to human gene names. Synaptic genes were identiﬁed using SynGO for the DEGs, using default settings81. To compare results of quantitative proteomics and RNA-seq results for the 2-week time point experiments, PADOG method in ReactomeGSA was used82. Per requirement of this method full gene and protein lists were used. Reactome was also used to identify pathways related to the DEGs, using the gene list analysis method, default setting was used including projecting to human identiﬁers. Gene ontology was conducted using metascape71. For differential splicing analysis raw FASTQ ﬁles for each experiment (4 h and 2 wk timepoints) were processed independently using the nf-core/rnasplice pipeline (version 1.0.4) executed via Nextﬂow on a SLURM-managed high-performance computing cluster with Singularity proﬁle. Raw reads underwent quality control with FastQC and were adapter-trimmed and quality-ﬁltered using Trim Galore! (via Cutadapt), with a NextSeq-speciﬁc poly-G trim parameter of 20 to remove low-quality bases and poly-Gtails.Good quality reads were alignmed to the Mus musculus reference genome (GRCm39 primary assembly, Ensembl release 113) using STAR for splice-aware mapping coupled with Salmon for quasi-mapping-based transcript quantiﬁcation (star_- salmon mode). Post-alignment, BAM ﬁles were sorted and indexed with SAMtools, and bigWig coverage ﬁles were generated using BED- Tools and ucsc-bedGraphToBigWig. Transcript-level quantiﬁcations from Salmon were imported and summarized to gene and transcript levels using tximport, yielding counts, TPM-normalized values, and scaled TPMs (dtuScaledTPM) for downstream analyzes. Differential splicing analysis employed rMATSturbo (integrated version) on STAR-aligned BAMs to detect ﬁve common alternative splicing event types: skipped exons (SE), alternative 5′ splice sites (A5SS), alternative 3′ splice sites (A3SS), mutually exclusive exons (MXE), and retained introns (RI). Exon inclusion was quantiﬁed as percent spliced in (PSI), with evaluations based on junction counts (JC) or junction counts plus exon body reads (JCEC). Statistically signiﬁcant events were ﬁltered by: read coverage ≥10 in both groups, | ΔPSI | ≥0.05, FDR ≤0.05, and exclusion of events with average PSI < 0.05 or >0.95 in both groups. Signiﬁcant events were visualized using rmats2sashimiplot (v 2.0.4), generating PDF ﬁles organized by event type and evaluation method (JC/JCEC). Differential transcript usage (DTU) was assessed using DRIMSeq for gene and feature ﬁltering, followed by DEXSeq (DTU mode enabled) to assess exon-level usage statistics, gene-level results via F tests and Simes method, and exon expression data. Additionally, scanRBP (v0.2) was applied to identify potential RNA-binding protein (RBP) motifs at splice junctions, querying 1272 motifs from mCross and CISBP-RNA databases against 80-nt regions ﬂanking splice donor sites, with binding vectors reported as log-odds ratios ( > 12 threshold).

Lysates were generated and processed as previously described in “label free nuclear proteomics”.

Thermal proteome proﬁling HEK293T or neuronal cell pellets were lysed in reticulocyte standard buffer containing 10 mM Tris-HCl, 15 mM NaCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, and 1x Halt protease inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc, 78438). Lysates were incubated on ice for 20 minutes followed by clariﬁcation via centrifugation at 17,000 × g for 30 minutes at 4 °C. Soluble fraction was transferred to microcentrifuge tube and protein concentration was measured by Pierce BCA protein assay (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc, 23225). Lysate was diluted to 1.5 mg/mL in lysis buffer and allowed to warm to room temperature. Cell lysates were treated with either DMSO or 1.5 µM SR-1815 in DMSO and allowed to incubate for 15 minutes at room temperature. Each treatment was then divided into 8 fractions in 200 µl PCR strip tubes and heated across a temperature gradient from 38 °C to 61 °C for 3 min on a thermocycler.Each fraction was allowed to cool to room temperature, transferred to a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube. Precipitated proteins were removed by centrifugation at 17,000 × g for 15 min. The soluble fractions were transferred to fresh 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes. Soluble fraction was then processed as previously described in “label free nuclear proteomics”.

Neuronal Western Blot Neurons were prepared and treated as indicated in neuronal proteomics. On DIV 14, plates were washed with PBS twice and proteins were extracted by sonication in a buffer consisting of 2% SDS, 50 mM Sodium Borate, 1X Halt Protease and Phosphatase inhibitors. Sample protein concentrations were measured using Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo: 23225) and adjusted to normalize protein content. 10 µg of protein per sample was loaded and separated by SDS-PAGE on 10% Criterion TGX Stain-Free gels (BioRad: 5678035), transferred to low ﬂuorescence PVDF membranes (45 µm pore size) (Amersham: GE10600004) with the Trans-Blot Turbo System (BioRad). Membranes were imaged for total protein using BioRad ChemiDoc imaging system, blocked with 1% BSA-TBS-T for 1 h, and then probed with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight. Membranes were washed 3X with TBS-T, incubated with secondary antibodies, washed, and imaged for chemiluminescence. Uncropped and unprocessed blots are included in the supplementary information and source data ﬁles.

Neuronal morphology and spine quantiﬁcation Neurons were isolated from Syngap1 constitutive (Syngap1+/-) mice and plated into 384-well plates at 15,000 neurons per well containing vehicle or SR-1815 at 1.5 µM83. Neurons were given 50% media exchanged containing vehicle or SR-1815 on DIV 7 and 10 ( + FUDR at DIV 7-14). Imaging was performed on DIV 14 using an IN Cell 6000 (20x magniﬁcation). Tracing data were obtained by imaging the entire well and stitched together using ImageJ. Dendritic morphology was traced using Fiji-ImageJ plugin Simple Neurite Tracer (SNT)79. A sample of 32 neurons per group were randomly selected and traced blinded. Data represent the average branch length in microns for all dendrites of the traced neuron. For spine density analysis, 2-3 dendrites were selected per traced neuron and spines were counted using SNT and normalized to dendritic length. Spine intensity was normalized to dendritic intensity.

KINOMEscanTM

We contracted Euroﬁns DiscoverX (Fremont, CA) to perform the scanMAX assay within the larger KINOMEscan™screening platform. KINOMEscan™assays do not require ATP and thereby report true thermodynamic interaction afﬁnities, as opposed to IC50 values, which can depend on the ATP concentration. The largest commercial kinase panel available, scanMAX contains a set of 468 kinases covering AGC, CAMK, CMGC, CK1, STE, TK, TKL, lipid and atypical kinase families, plus important mutant forms. scanMAX is an ideal choice for all stages of drug discovery and development, from lead discovery & hit identiﬁcation to lead optimization, preclinical and compound safety. Kinome-wide annotation of compound selectivity enables informed decisions about therapeutic opportunities and potential offtarget liabilities which could otherwise be missed in smaller kinase panels. This panel includes: 453 human kinases, 3 pathogen kinases, 56 disease relevant mutants, 132 tyrosine kinase assays, and 20 lipid kinases.

Kinase assays For most assays, kinase-tagged T7 phage strains were grown in parallel in 24-well blocks in an E. coli host derived from the BL21 strain. E. coli were grown to log-phase and infected with T7 phage from a frozen stock (multiplicity of infection = 0.4) and incubated with shaking at 32 °C until lysis (90-150 min). The lysates were centrifuged (6,000 x g) and ﬁltered (0.2 μm) to remove cell debris. The remaining kinases were produced in HEK-293 cells and subsequently tagged with DNA for qPCR detection. Streptavidin-coated magnetic beads were treated with biotinylated small molecule ligands for 30 min at room temperature to generate afﬁnity resins for kinase assays. The liganded beads were blocked with excess biotin and washed with blocking

buffer (SeaBlock (Pierce), 1 % BSA, 0.05 % Tween 20, 1 mM DTT) to remove unbound ligand and to reduce non-speciﬁc phage binding. Binding reactions were assembled by combining kinases, liganded afﬁnity beads, and test compounds in 1x binding buffer (20 % SeaBlock, 0.17x PBS, 0.05 % Tween 20, 6 mM DTT). Test compounds were prepared as 100x stocks in 100% DMSO and directly diluted into the assay. All reactions were performed in polypropylene 384-well plates in a ﬁnal volume of 0.02 mL. The assay plates were incubated at room temperature with shaking for 1 h and the afﬁnity beads were washed with wash buffer (1x PBS, 0.05 % Tween 20). The beads were then resuspended in elution buffer (1x PBS, 0.05 % Tween 20, 0.5 μM nonbiotinylated afﬁnity ligand) and incubated at room temperature with shaking for 30 min. The kinase concentration in the eluates was measured by qPCR.

Selectivity score (S-scores) Selectivity Score or S-score is a quantitative measure of compound selectivity. It is calculated by dividing the number of kinases that compounds bind to by the total number of distinct kinases tested, excluding mutant variants.
